Keynote #1 - Dr. Petra Kuhnert
Chair: Angela Anderson
Details
Irresponsible use of AI is a Crime Scene: sifting through the slop to deliver responsible AI solutions
Dr. Petra Kuhnert
Abstract

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is moving at a rapid pace, shaping decisions across sectors and communities. As a result, the number of paper submissions to leading AI venues has surged. For example, in 2025, a little over 71,000 papers were submitted to the main research track of five of the top machine learning conferences, representing a 32% increase since 24 and a 10-fold increase from ten years ago. This rise in volume is becoming increasingly difficult to manage and consume in the academic community. Alongside genuine advances, there is also work that is incremental, overly tuned to curated benchmarks, weakly evidenced or even AI-generated without adequate verification.

If we want AI research and deployed systems that are trusted, robust and transparent, we need a forensic lens on how AI and its underlying analytics are developed and evaluated. For me, Statistics provides that lens, yet it can be sidelined in the rush to publish AI and deploy.

In this talk, I use the metaphor of a crime scene to describe AI crime: errors in predictions, uncertainty and inference that lead to poor decisions and in high-stakes settings can translate into real-world harm. I outline what Responsible, Application-Driven AI (RAD-AI) looks like in practice, and the statistical checks and incentives that help prevent failure modes and AI crime before it reaches the field. I will illustrate these ideas with work we are developing with stakeholders to produce a trusted AI crop growth model.

We would not cut corners at a crime scene, so why would we allow crime to happen with AI!

Biography

Dr. Petra Kuhnert is a Senior Principal Research Scientist at CSIRO and an expert at the intersection of statistics and machine learning. Her work develops methodology for risk-based decision-making in environmental and agricultural applications where she develops methods that are fit for purpose, relevant to the question at hand, and usable by decision-makers.

Her work, particularly supporting Great Barrier Reef decision-making, has been recognised through awards including 1st Runner Up (APAC Women in AI Innovator of the Year, 2023) and the APAC Women in AI Award for Environment and Biodiversity (2023).

A key contribution to AI-driven decision-making is her award-winning software Vizumap, an R package that helps users understand and communicate uncertainty on maps.

More recently, her focus has included machine-learning emulators to speed up slow-running physical system models, Bayesian methods for decision support, and approaches that use geospatial data (e.g., remote sensing) to improve prediction of terrestrial environmental and agricultural processes. Her previous roles include Associate Science Director for University Engagement and Group Leader of the Statistical Machine Learning Group in CSIRO’s Data61.

She has co-authored 100+ journal articles, with 6,000+ citations and a Google Scholar h-index of 30+. Her collaborations span leading government departments, universities and industry.

Genstat Markdown: Reproducible Research with Genstat
James Curran
Abstract

Reproducible research ensures that scientific findings can be independently verified by others using the same data and methods. Markdown plays a key role in supporting reproducibility by allowing researchers to combine code, results, and narrative text in a clear, lightweight format. Tools like R Markdown or Jupyter Notebooks use Markdown to embed executable code alongside explanations and outputs, making it easy to document workflows, share analyses, and regenerate results consistently across different environments.

Genstat is a statistical software package designed for data analysis, particularly in biometrical research and applications. Many users know it through its user-friendly interface. However, it also It offers a powerful scripting language.

In this talk I will describe a collaborative project between students and staff at the University of Auckland and VSNi Ltd, that allows Genstat to be used in conjunction with R Markdown to provide flexible reproducible research capability to the Genstat user community.

Biography

My research focuses on statistical problems in forensic science, particularly the interpretation of DNA, and trace evidence. More broadly, I enjoy developing statistical methods and practical tools motivated by real-world problems.

Leveraging the core: R Shiny apps which talk to the Genstat Engine

Abstract

Genstat is a statistical software package designed for data analysis, particularly in bioscience research and its applications. While many users are familiar with its user-friendly interface, it also provides a powerful scripting language for advanced statistical computing.

11:00-11:15
Pizzas, Biometry and the 5Rs
Mario D’Antuono
Abstract

In 2008, at the Australasian Genstat Users Association (AGUA) meeting, then known as the Genstat Conference in Marysville, Victoria, I presented a controversial paper on my forthcoming e-book entitled “Biometry: The 5Rs”.

The paper was controversial because it presented an argument that in 5 simple lines of code using the R Statistical System (denoted by R) usually in the form of a function call, I could address a task such as the generation of a near-optimal design, or a statistical analysis. These 5 lines can be recursive and hence can call other functions within a function (a nested approach). The approach was stimulated by the work of Karl Broman at the time and his 3Rs (Reproducible Research with R).

In 2019, I retired from the Department of Agriculture, Western Australia. It has taken 7 years for me to find the time and the energy to complete the e-book. The free R software to handle the above has developed to be able to treat many of the common problems in agricultural research.

We illustrate two published examples from the literature, which are case-studies in the e-book; the first involves the construction of a near-optimal p-rep design, and the second, a spatial linear mixed model analysis. We compare the results from the University of Wollongong R packages dwreml-R and odw-R (soon to be released on GitHub) with other software such as CycDesign, speed-R, and DiGGer-R for near-optimal design generation, and asreml-R and Echidna for linear mixed modelling.

Biography

Mario worked as a biometrician in the Biometrics Unit of the WA Dept of Agriculture (now known as DPIRD) from 1977 to 2019. He was President of the Australasian Region of the International Biometric Society (IBS-AR) 2011-2012. He was a long-time Genstat and CycDesign user, and was heavily involved in the Genstat conference, Busselton December 2002, and the IBS-AR meetings held in December 2011 at Kiama, NSW, and the first and only IBS-AR meeting held in Western Australia so far (December 2013 at Mandurah).

11:15-11:30
A modified PQL method for genetic analysis of binary variables
Arthur Gilmour
Abstract

In plant and animal breeding, there is the need to estimate breeding values for binary traits such as lamb survival and presence/absence of disease. For such traits, the average incidence is often outside [0.2, 0.8] and it varies with known fixed effects and covariates. Animal breeders commonly assume the binary trait is based on an underlying normal liability exceeding a threshold. PQL (pseudo quasi-likelihood), an extension of GLM to include random effects in the linear model, is commonly used to analyse such data and predict breeding values, but is known to underestimate the heritability when fitting an animal model. It iterates using a working variable \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{\eta} + (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{\mu})/\delta\), where \(\mathbf{\eta}\) is the prediction on the liability scale (\(\mathbf{X\beta}+\mathbf{Zu}\)), \(\mathbf{y}\) is binary outcome, \(\mathbf{\mu} = f(\mathbf{\eta})\) is predicted mean on the probability scale, \(\delta\) is the derivative of the probit link function \(f(\eta)\), \(\mathbf{X}\) is the design matrix for fixed effects (\(\mathbf{\beta}\)) and \(\mathbf{Z}\) is the design matrix for random effects (\(\mathbf{u}\)). The linear model,\(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{X\beta} + \mathbf{Zu} + \mathbf{e}\) is fitted with weights \(δ^2/\)var(\(y\)), var(\(y\)) is \(\mu(1-\mu)\). The mPQL model, in the simplest case, calculates \(\mathbf{\eta} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta}\), leading to changes in \(\mu\) and \(\delta\), and necessitates estimating a dispersion factor when fitting the linear model (which is unchanged). My recommendation when using mPQL is first to fit the model on the probability scale, note the mean (\(p\)), calculate the heritability (\(h_o^2\)), the dispersion factor \(((1 - h_o^2)\) and predict an approximate heritability for the liability scale using \(h_l^2 = h_o^2 p(1-p)/z^2\). Then, fit the mPQL model using the dispersion factor. mPQL is available in Echidna (EchidnaMMS.org)

Biography

Arthur Gilmour worked for NSW Agriculture as a biometrician from 1970 to 2008. He is currently contracted part time to VSN International to support ASReml.

11:30-11:45
ggincerta: An R package for Uncertainty Visualisation with a Layered Grammar of Graphics
Maggie Ma
Abstract

A key challenge in spatial visualisation is the simultaneous communication of estimated values and their associated uncertainties, as visual channels are occupied by spatial structure, leaving limited capacity to encode additional information. We developed ggincerta, an R package that extends the layered grammar of graphics implemented in ggplot2, to facilitate the visualisation of uncertainty in spatial data. Through its native integration with ggplot2, ggincerta enables users to leverage the full flexibility of the grammar of graphics to create complex and customised visualisations through simpler and more consistent workflows in spatial and more general data settings. In addition to reproducing existing uncertainty visualisation techniques, the package introduces new approaches, including the dual map, a visualisation designed to support selective attention between estimated values and their associated uncertainties. We demonstrate the capabilities of ggincerta through several case studies, illustrating how the package can be used to create informative and visually effective maps that communicate both estimates and uncertainty, while also highlighting relevant technical details and visual features. By integrating uncertainty visualisation directly into the ggplot2 ecosystem and expanding the range of available uncertainty displays, ggincerta provides a flexible and powerful framework for researchers and practitioners working with spatial and other information-rich data.

Biography

Maggie Ma is a PhD student in Statistics at the Australian National University. Her research focuses on statistical graphics, spatial data visualisation, and the communication of uncertainty. She is currently developing the R package ggincerta, which extends the ggplot2 framework with specialised layers and scales for visualising uncertainty in geospatial data.

11:45-12:00
torch-openreml: a PyTorch-based framework for flexible linear mixed-effects modelling
Patrick Li
Abstract

We introduce torch-openreml, a PyTorch-based Python library under active early development for fitting linear mixed-effects models using the Average Information Restricted Maximum Likelihood (AI-REML) algorithm. The library represents covariance models as compositional computation graphs, where complex covariance structures are constructed by combining modular components through algebraic operations.

Within this framework, model parameters can be fixed, estimated, or transformed, with analytical gradients provided where possible and PyTorch automatic differentiation used for general cases. The AI-REML solver exploits common covariance structures to improve computational efficiency and benefits from PyTorch support for CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators.

Although currently in an early alpha stage, torch-openreml supports a wide range of linear mixed-effects modelling applications, such as multi-environment trial analysis, spatial modelling, and genomic prediction. It enables rapid prototyping of novel covariance models without requiring manual gradient derivation, providing an extensible platform for modern mixed-effects modelling.

Biography

Dr Weihao (Patrick) Li is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Research School of Finance, Actuarial Studies and Statistics, Australian National University. He holds a PhD in Statistics from Monash University. His research in the Analytics for the Australian Grains Industry (AAGI) project focuses on machine learning, image analytics, and plant phenotyping.

12:00-12:15
One Workflow, Many Questions: A Unified Workflow for Statistical Modelling in the Age of AI
Kathrin Schemann
Abstract

Applied statisticians increasingly work across diverse modelling paradigms, each with distinct assumptions, methods, and reporting requirements. At the same time, the rapid emergence of AI tools creates opportunities to improve efficiency while raising important questions about transparency, reproducibility, and statistical rigor.

This presentation introduces a practical, software-agnostic workflow developed at the Statistical Consulting Unit of the Sydney Informatics Hub, The University of Sydney. The workflow provides a unified framework for addressing descriptive, predictive, and causal modelling objectives while maintaining focus on fundamental statistical principles and research context. The framework follows a shared structure that begins with clearly defining the research question, identifying variables of interest, documenting assumptions, and developing a transparent analysis plan. Key components include study design, bias assessment, variable selection, interaction assessment, model evaluation, interpretation, and communication of results. The presentation also examines how AI can be integrated throughout the analytical process, supporting tasks such as planning, coding, documentation, model implementation, diagnostic review, and reporting. Within the workflow, AI is positioned as a tool to augment—not replace—statistical expertise, subject-matter knowledge, and professional judgment.

By combining established statistical principles with structured opportunities for AI augmentation, the workflow provides a consistent approach to applied statistical practice across modelling objectives, supporting more transparent, reproducible, efficient, and impactful research.

Biography

Kathrin is a Senior Statistical Consultant and leads the operations of the Statistical Consulting Unit at the Sydney Informatics Hub (University of Sydney). With 15+ years of broad, applied experience in academia and public health, she develops practical workflows to empower researchers with robust statistical skills, particularly in optimising analytical design for higher impact research.

12:15-12:30
Nested-factorial treatment models: types, their uses and examples
Chris Brien
Abstract

Most commonly factorial experiments involve several crossed treatment factors and the treatment model includes terms for all possible combinations of the treatment factors. However, treatment models that employ nested treatment factors are beneficial in a number of situations and could be used more often. Applicable situations include those in which (i) treatment factors are intrinsically nested, (ii) treatments involve one or more factors plus a control and (iii) treatments have been systematically allocated and/or are pseudoreplicated. Four basic types of nested factors that start with a single nesting factor are (i) one nested factor, (ii) multiple, crossed, nested factors, (iii) multiple, independent, nested factors, and (iv) a hierarchy of multiple, nested factors. Examples involving the different situations and types of nesting will be presented. Constructing the factors using the R package dae (Brien, 2026, https://cran.r-project.org/package=dae) will be described and the properties of the models discussed for the examples via their anatomies produced using dae.

Biography

I am a part-time Senior Biometrician in the Plant Accelerator, at Adelaide University where I consult and carry out statistical research. My main interests are in experiment design and linear mixed model analysis, especially for multiphase experiments. In the last 10 years, the design and analysis of plant phenotyping data has become a particular focus. I also maintain three R packages on CRAN.

Keynote #2 - Dr. Salvador Gezan
Chair: Michael Mumford
Details
Fitting Large Genomic Models: Computational Strategies and Approximations within the Linear Mixed Model Framework
Dr. Salvador Gezan
Abstract

As genomic datasets grow larger, substantial statistical and computational challenges arise when analysing single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data. Such data are widely used in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS), Polygenic Risk Score (PRS) analyses, and genome-wide prediction models. Depending on the field and context, it is common to encounter datasets containing millions of SNPs and hundreds of thousands of genotyped individuals. Fitting even the simplest linear mixed model at this scale is computationally demanding, requiring the handling of large genomic matrices and the estimation of a large number of marker effects. Statistical and mathematical techniques such as Cholesky decomposition, eigen-transformation, Singular Value Decomposition, and low-rank matrix approximations provide practical solutions for fitting these models and obtaining the required effects and predictions. This talk will present key mathematical details, illustrations, and practical guidelines for addressing large-scale genomic analyses in plant and animal breeding.

Biography

Salvador Gezan is a statistician and quantitative geneticist with over 20 years of experience, currently serving as a Statistical Genetics Consultant at VSN International. He specialises in mixed models and their application to biological problems, supporting agricultural, forestry, and aquaculture breeding programmes through the analysis of phenotypic and genotypic data, the development of breeding strategies, and the implementation of genomic selection in operational breeding programmes. He began his career at Rothamsted Research, was an Associate Professor at the University of Florida, and has delivered ASReml workshops globally. Dr. Gezan has over 160 peer-reviewed publications and is a co-author of Statistical Methods in Biology: Design and Analysis of Experiments and Regression.

14:30-14:45
Predicting Cotton Fibre Performance using GWAS Summary Statistics
Qian Feng
Abstract

Genomic prediction (GP) refers to the prediction of individual’s phenotypes using genome-wide information. In humans, GP has contributed substantially to the development of precision medicine, while in animal and plant breeding it has accelerated genetic gain by enabling earlier and more accurate selection. Traditional GP methods rely on individual-level genotype and phenotype data, which are often subject to privacy, ownership and data sharing restrictions. Recently, summary-statistics-based methods have emerged for GP by leveraging genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics and linkage disequilibrium information from a reference population. These approaches avoid the need of individual-level data and have been widely applied in human genetics. However, their application in plant breeding, including cotton, remains very limited. Here, we investigate the feasibility of summary-statistics-based genomic prediction using a large-scale cotton dataset collected over 40 year-site combinations in central-eastern Australia. Both genotype and phenotype data are available for this dataset, enabling the computation of GWAS summary statistics and a direct comparison between conventional Genomic Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (GBLUP) and a summary-statistics-based BLUP approach. Our empirical results show that the two methods achieve comparable prediction accuracy across multiple fibre yield and quality traits, consistent with theoretical expectations. We further evaluate how the choice of reference population and GWAS summary statistics information influences prediction performance. These results demonstrate the potential of summary-statistics-based GP in cotton and suggest that this approach could enable the use of larger, more diverse publicly available datasets to support the development of better cotton varieties.

Biography

Qian Feng is a CERC research fellow at CSIRO Agriculture and Food Unit. Her current research focuses on designing and implementing statistical methods to accelerate the breeding of Australian rain-grown cotton. She also interests in detecting evolutionary processes from pathogen and human genomes, including the recombination identification with hidden Markov models.

14:45-15:00
Protein Advantage for Mungbean in Australia
Jodine O’Connor
Abstract

The growing emphasis on plant-based diets and the increasing demand for protein have brought pulse grains into sharp focus. As the second-largest exporter of pulse grains globally, Australia is uniquely positioned to meet this rising demand. To maintain market share and leverage the growing interest in plant-based protein, the Grains Research and Development Corporation (GRDC) and Agriculture Victoria have initiated a national project aimed at exploring innovative strategies to support and expand this vital industry. The project focuses on six pulse crops: mungbean, chickpea, lupin, lentil, faba bean and field pea. To date, historical varieties for each crop have been evaluated across Australia’s major pulse growing regions. These trials span 33 sites across five states, conducted in 2024 and 2025. With demand to meeting new markets, a challenge arises for breeding varieties that achieve both high yield and desirable protein levels. Therefore, a statistical methodology is proposed with a protein advantage metric. Using available mungbean data, a multi-environment, across-year bivariate analysis was performed for three sites in QLD and NSW. This analysis examined yield and protein content within a bivariate linear mixed model framework, extended to incorporate multi-environment data. The framework also included spatial modelling for each trial and factor analytic modelling to allow for heterogeneous genetic covariance across trials. The bivariate analysis revealed a strong negative genetic correlation between yield and protein content across all environments. The protein advantage metric was obtained by using genotype deviations from the regression line between protein and yield. When plotted, varieties with a positive protein advantage or a negative advantage are clearly identified. This information provides valuable insights for growers and pulse breeders to select varieties that align with targeted market traits (e.g. protein) and production goals in Australia.

Biography

My career began in animal breeding and genetics before progressing into plant breeding. I enjoy experimental design and analysis of Multiple Environment Trials (MET) incorporating pedigree information across many commercial crops using ASReml-R. My interests include pedigree analysis, image analysis, marker data analysis, data management and working with industry to streamline research outcomes.

15:30-15:45
Identifying cellular relationships in finely annotated spatial transcriptomics data
Ellis Patrick
Abstract

Recent cell-resolution spatial transcriptomics technologies enable whole-transcriptome profiling of millions of individual cells within intact tissues, creating unprecedented opportunities to study how cellular organisation varies across development, health and disease. However, the same resolution that makes these data biologically powerful also makes them analytically fragile. Although these assays target approximately 20,000 genes, each cell typically contains only a sparse sample of detected transcripts, with measurements also contaminated by transcript diffusion, imperfect segmentation and cell overlap. This makes expression estimates uncertain and can destabilise fine-grained cell labels. Fine-grained labels can also fragment the data into rare populations for which spatial associations are difficult to estimate precisely. Inference on spatial organisation is further complicated by correlation at multiple scales, arising from cohort design, tissue sampling and the spatial arrangement of cells within structured anatomical regions. Together, measurement error, annotation uncertainty and dependence can produce unstable estimates and reduced power for detecting meaningful spatial relationships.

In this talk, I will present approaches developed by my team to address these challenges in high-dimensional spatial omics data. Using hierarchical modelling, cluster-robust variance estimation, bootstrapping and weighting strategies, we developed more robust and powerful tests for spatial association under annotation uncertainty and multiscale dependence. These methods support inference across cell-cell association testing, proximity-associated gene programs, rare-cell localisation and multicellular tissue architecture, providing a framework for extracting reliable biological signal from sparse, contaminated and correlated spatial omics data.

Biography

Ellis Patrick is an Associate Professor in the School of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Sydney and Cluster Lead of Bioinformatics in the Sydney Precision Data Science Centre. His research develops statistical methods and software for spatial omics and other emerging biomedical technologies, helping researchers better understand human disease.

15:45-16:00
A Location-Scale Linked Autoregressive Moving Average Model for Wind Direction Time Series Data
Piumi Perera
Abstract

Modelling long-term wind direction time series data poses several challenges, including the circular nature of the observations, temporal processes operating at multiple scales, and the need to jointly capture both mean direction and variability in the presence of serial dependence. Motivated by hourly wind direction observations collected between 2013 and 2016 from a Bureau of Meteorology station in Broome, Western Australia, we propose a location-scale linked autoregressive moving average (LSLARMA) model that prioritises interpretability and data generation. The proposed framework adopts a two-stage approach, comprising a location-scale regression applied to transformed wind direction, followed by a (seasonal) ARMA model fitted to the resulting quantile residuals to capture remaining serial dependence. Application of the LSLARMA model reveals clear annual, monthly, and diurnal patterns in both the mean and dispersion of wind direction. In addition, the model can generate realistic synthetic time series that reproduce key features of the observed wind direction data, while compared with alternative single stage approaches the proposed method delivers improved performance and greater interpretability of the underlying temporal processes.

Biography

Piumi Perera is a PhD student in Statistics at the Australian National University. Their research focuses primarily on modelling circular responses and environmental data. 

16:00-16:15
Cross trial analysis of rotation by environment interaction in the Western Australian Farming Systems project
Ben Nestor
Abstract

The Western Australian Farming Systems (WAFS) project involves ongoing trials comparing four-year standard and diverse cropping rotations under two nitrogen supply levels (low and high). Trials are located across three WA cropping environments: Northampton (northern, medium rainfall), Merredin (eastern, low rainfall), and Lake Grace (southern, medium rainfall). Rotations include combinations of cereals, canola, grain legumes, manured legumes, multi-species, and fallow with different phasings of rotations. A multi-environment trial (MET) analysis was performed to investigate rotation x environment interactions, with environment defined as the combination of location and nitrogen treatment. The relative performance of each rotation was compared across environments using gross profit margins from three years of rotations as the response variable in a factor analytic model. The best linear unbiased predictions were compared across rotations to identify rotation types that were most profitable in different environments and rotation types that gave more consistent profits across environments. This analysis demonstrates a novel application of MET analysis on cropping rotation trials, providing insights into the effects of rotation and nitrogen treatment across different WA agricultural environments.

Biography

I completed a PhD in plant bioinformatics at the University of Western Australia in 2024 and joined DPIRD as a Biometrics Research Scientist later that year. At DPIRD, I have contributed to a range of agricultural, horticultural, and rangeland research projects and my work generally involves trial analyses and experimental design, multi-environment trial analyses, and multivariate analyses.

16:15-16:30
A quantitative framework for dissecting genotype by environment interactions driving crop yield variability
Stephanie Brunner
Abstract

Climate change magnifies unpredictable environmental patterns, threatening global crop yields. A wide range of approaches exist to assess varieties across environments through mixed linear models with latent or environmental variables. However, the underlying causes of these genotype by environment interactions (GEIs) remain unexplored. Understanding how genetic and environmental factors interact to drive yield variation is critical for breeding resilient crops. This research develops a framework to investigate the genetic and environmental drivers of GEI to help inform crop breeding decisions. Real world breeding program data was used to develop this framework, ensuring practical applicability. A panel of 965 lines of barley germplasm was evaluated for yield in 12 trials. To dissect the genetic component of GEI a genomic mixed linear model was fitted in which random genetic effects were structured by a genomic relationship matrix leveraging shared genetic information to predict yield across environments. To interpret these predictions biologically, haplotype effects were estimated for marker effects allowing for yield to be explored at the haplotype level. Haplotypes with large GEI for yield were found to have different effects across different environments. The environmental component of GEI was explored using a synthetic environmental covariate approach, which represents major environmental gradients as linear combinations of measured variables (e.g. rainfall). This method attributes GEI variance to interpretable environmental covariates at key growth stages, providing a measure of stability across time. This temporal deconstruction of GEI variance allowed for the analysis of the impact of individual environmental covariates on haplotype effects for yield bridging the two components of this research. This framework helps to disentangle GEIs and identify environment-responsive haplotypes enabling breeders to target yield stability despite climatic uncertainty.

Biography

Final year PhD student at the University of Queensland interested in exploring novel methodology for practical applications in plant breeding specifically modelling of genotype by environment interactions.

17:00-19:00
Details
Modelling plant growth for biological discovery
Andrew Bowerman
Abstract

High-throughput plant phenotyping platforms, such as those in the Australian Plant Phenomics Network, generate dense, repeated measurements of plant growth over time. Extracting biologically meaningful information from these growth trajectories is not straightforward: mechanistic models require an explicit functional form to be specified in advance, which is often laborious to define and fit separately for each genotype or treatment, particularly when growth is irregular or environmentally responsive. We explore statistical approaches, including Gaussian processes and spline-based models, as a flexible alternative for characterising growth trajectories from phenomics data, without requiring a pre-specified functional form. These methods can accommodate nonlinear and irregular growth patterns directly from the data, while still yielding interpretable summaries such as growth rate, timing of key developmental transitions, and genotype- or treatment-level variation. Gaussian processes further provide a natural measure of uncertainty around these estimates, which is valuable when growth trajectories are noisy or unevenly sampled. We present this as a complementary approach to mechanistic modelling, rather than a replacement for it. Statistical characterisation of growth trajectories can help identify patterns that are worth investigating mechanistically, flagging where and when a genotype or treatment departs from expected growth, for example. Because these methods do not require a model to be fitted individually to each genotype or treatment, they are also well suited to the scale of modern phenomics platforms. In this way, statistical modelling offers a practical route to turning large-scale phenotypic data into biological insight.

Biography

Dr Andrew Bowerman is a quantitative biologist at ANU, working at the interface of plant physiology and statistics. His research spans chloroplast retrograde signalling, wheat field trial analysis, and mixed-model approaches to complex phenotypic data. Drawing on a background in both molecular biology and wheat physiology, he translates quantitative models into biologically meaningful discovery.

A Statistical Framework for Data Streams
Bao Khue Tran
Abstract

Data streams are potentially unbounded sequences of observations that must be processed incrementally under strict memory and time constraints. Despite their ubiquity, streaming data currently lack a coherent statistical foundation as most existing work is computer science-focused. This raises fundamental questions: How should a data stream be represented as a statistical object? Which classical properties carry over to the streaming setting, and which require reformulation? How can competing methods for the same inferential target be compared?

We propose a rigorous and comprehensive framework for evaluating streaming methods. Using a running example examined at increasing levels of complexity, we show how each layer of our framework addresses gaps in existing approaches, and what is required to perform rigorous statistical inference on data streams.

Biography

Bao Khue Tran is a PhD candidate in the School of Mathematics and Statistics at UNSW Sydney, supervised by Pierre Lafaye De Micheaux and Gery Geenens. Her research develops rigorous statistical frameworks for streaming data analysis, and she is keen to connect on real-world streaming applications. She also teaches statistics at UNSW, from first-year to master’s level.

Quantifying Spatial Variation in Injury-Related Bloodstream Infections across Queensland
Binuri Perera
Abstract

Bloodstream infection (BSI) is a serious complication among injured patients. Although injury- related BSI are known to vary across broader remoteness categories in Queensland, the local variations within small areas are yet unknown. This study aimed to examine the disparities in residential location among people with injury-related BSIs in Queensland using population-based linked data.

The linked used data for this study consists of patient admission data from Queensland Hospital Admitted Patient Data Collection (QHAPDC), pathology data and death data from the Death Registry for Queenslanders from 2010 to 2019. Aggregated data on acute injury hospital episodes and estimated residential population were used to calculate incidence rates. Leroux models were fitted to examine the spatial variations using standardised incidence ratios. Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations were used to fit the models.

Across the entire 10-year period, 1,895 people experienced an injury-related BSI. There was marked spatial variation across the state, with particularly high rates observed in northern, far north and western Queensland. Consistent patterns were observed after accounting for the injury hospitalisations.

Bayesian spatial models enable the identification of high-risk areas with higher incidence based on patients’ residential location. The results are beneficial for medical staff and policymakers in identifying disparities based on location and implementing targeted interventions and service improvements.

Biography

Binuri Perera is a Biostatistician and Spatial Epidemiologist at Queensland University of Technology, investigating injury-related bloodstream infections using linked population health data. Her research applies spatial, spatio-temporal and survival analyses to examine geographic inequities in incidence and outcomes.

Efficient feature detection in spiky data using penalised effects in a linear mixed model
Clayton Forknall
Abstract

Analysing spiky data, where spiky refers to a response variable that demonstrates severe variation in magnitude in response to one or more explanatory variables, requires care, with challenges arising both in terms of feature detection and model assumptions. We propose a linear mixed model (LMM) based approach for the analysis of spiky data arising from designed experiments. The approach utilises penalties, applied both to the random effects of interest, along with the residual errors, to i) efficiently detect and estimate important features in the response and ii) allow for more flexible t-distributed errors. The approach is motivated by, and demonstrated using, a dataset arising from a mass spectrometry based proteomics experiment, where our aim is to efficiently detect significant peptides and/or proteins that are present at different stages of the barley malting process. Our approach is easily implementable in most LMM software packages, providing a readily applicable solution to a challenging and complex problem.

Biography

Clayton is a Senior Biometrician with The Plant Accelerator, a Node of the Australian Plant Phenomics Network, at Adelaide University. He is also currently working to complete his PhD part time at The University of Queensland. Clayton enjoys the challenge of being an applied statistician, working with researchers to solve complex problems facing the agricultural industry.

Improved assessment of rangeland management
Damian Collins
Abstract

Rangelands suitable for pastoral land use cover 50% of the earth’s terrestrial surface. Managing rangelands to reduce or avoid degradation is crucial for food production and ecological sustainability. In recent decades, the use of remote sensing has automated the monitoring of land condition, in particular ground cover, at higher spatial resolution, greater frequency, and lower cost than field surveys. Easier monitoring also allows improved assessment of changes in rangeland management. Assessing these impacts is complicated by climatic drivers of plant growth, especially rainfall and temperature. Methods to discriminate the effects of management on ground cover from climatic effects include regional comparison benchmarking (e.g. Donohue et al. (2022)), reference benchmarking (e.g. Bastin et al. (2012)) or predicted benchmarking approaches such as RESTREND (Evans & Geerken (2004)). Regional comparison and reference benchmarking both compare managed areas to reference areas or pixels. Predicted benchmarking approaches seek to standardise against climatic drivers of growth. This is done independently for each pixel by modelling the time series of ground cover against climatic data time series. To allow for lagged effects of rainfall and temperature, derived climate predictors with various lag and accumulation periods might be derived and the best one(s) selected by comparing \(R^2\) values, for instance. After accounting for climatic effects on ground cover, any remaining trends are interpreted as resulting from land management. We consider if the predicted benchmarking approach can be enhanced with alternative statistical tools. For instance, distributed lag models could predict the effects of climatic drivers with higher accuracy. In addition, pixels could be analysed in a spatio-temporal model instead of independently.

Biography

Damian Collins has worked as a biometrician at NSW DPIRD since 1996, based at Menangle (S-W Sydney). His main experience is in mixed models for agricultural data (PhD 2009 UoW, Estimation methods for GLMMs). His other interests include data visualisation, statistical communication, the R statistical software, and Linux (Fedora).

Improvements to macadamia crop yield forecasts by incorporating machine learning in model ensembles
Daniel Powell
Abstract

Crop yield forecasting forms an important component of strategic decision-making for the Australian macadamia industry. With growing pressures from challenging economic conditions, reliable forecasts assist in scheduling, logistics planning, and maintaining market confidence and price stability.

A range of highly variable and often interrelated environmental, economic and biological data sources are considered in developing predictions which create challenges in dealing with high dimensionality and covariance. And although past approaches implementing statistical forecasting models have achieved a high level of success, the intricate nature of influencing factors including climate, management practices, and varietal differences, invites efforts to explore further improvement to the accuracy of the forecasts.

Machine Learning (ML) methods have been shown to outperform other approaches in crop forecasting applications and, having advantages over traditional statistical models in their relaxed assumptions and flexibility to handle many more parameters, appear well suited to address this problem. We present our approach to incorporating ML in predicting crop yields and discuss some of the considerations in adopting these methods in tree crop forecasting. We also highlight the performance of a selection of ML methods used in recent crop estimates for macadamia production in Australia.

Biography

Daniel Powell is a scientist in the Emerging Technologies business unit of Agri-Science Queensland. Prior to this position he has spent over 15 years in universities in Australia and Sweden conducting research in agriculture and conservation.

To average or not? Analysis of quadrat-level BOTANAL data in grazing experiments.
David Reid
Abstract

This study was motivated by the analysis of data collected from central Queensland properties as part of the Queensland Pasture Resilience Program, a partnership between the Department of Primary Industries, Meat & Livestock Australia (MLA) and the Australian Government through the MLA Donor Company. Pasture yield and composition were assessed using the BOTANAL pasture method (Tothill et al., 1978), which involves visually rating quadrats (typically 30–200 per plot), and calibrating these ratings with an equation derived from a set of ratings and corresponding cut quadrat weights to estimate dry matter yield (kg/ha).

The experiment utilised a split-plot design with three replicates, P fertiliser (+/-) as the main-plot factor, five pasture treatments as sub-plots, and 32 quadrats (samples) per sub-plot. Alternative approaches to analysis were considered, including modelling at the quadrat level or using quadrat-averaged responses at the sub-plot level. Diagnostic residual plots indicated skewness and heteroscedasticity at the quadrat level, while assumptions were adequately met at the sub-plot (treatment) level, which corresponds to the experimental unit level.

These observations raise several practical questions: Is it appropriate to average the quadrat data given potential non-normality in this stratum? Will simply calculating sub-plot means be sufficient to allow a valid analysis? Are such concerns less important given the semi-quantitative nature of BOTANAL data, which rely on subjective ratings calibrated via fitted relationships between scores and observed dry matter?

This paper examines these issues and discusses the implications. In summary, averaging the quadrats is acceptable if skewness is mild/moderate with the quadrat distribution not biasing the mean severely, particularly given the subjectiveness of the data. However, if skewness is severe then apply the appropriate transformation (e.g. log transformation).

Biography

David Reid is a Principal Biometrician in the Animal Science business unit of Agri-Science Queensland with almost 40 years’ experience as a consulting biometrician, providing statistical direction and leadership for project teams across various agricultural industries. He has expertise in statistical design, analysis, interpretation and reporting.

Bayesian Variable Selection in Quantile Regression to Assess Joint Impacts of Climate Indices on Monthly Rainfall
Dilani Kaveendri Dambure Hewage
Abstract

Understanding how large-scale climate indices influence rainfall variability is important for assessing drought and flood risk in eastern Australia. This study examines the dependency between the joint impact of the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), Dipole Mode Index (DMI), and monthly rainfall quantiles in New South Wales (NSW), Australia, with particular emphasis on the tails of the monthly rainfall distribution. To address this, we employ a hierarchical model that incorporates Bayesian variable selection within a spatial quantile regression framework, allowing for the integration of two climate indices and spatial variation in their impacts on different parts of the monthly rainfall distribution. The first level of hierarchy expresses the asymmetric Laplace distribution as a location-scale mixture. The second level expresses the prior of the regression coefficients as a two-component mixture, with components being a point mass at zero and a normal distribution. The third level incorporates spatial dependence by modelling the joint inclusion probabilities of SOI and DMI using multinomial logistic regression, where the argument of the link function varies spatially according to a Gaussian Process prior. The results show that SOI is the dominant driver of monthly rainfall variability across NSW, with strong impacts in winter and spring and a notable impact across all quantiles in November. DMI has an important influence during spring, particularly September and October, across multiple quantiles. The lower and upper quantiles show greater sensitivity to SOI and DMI than the median in selected months and locations. DMI also shows an apparent influence at lower quantiles in January and March, suggesting an effect on drier conditions. These results demonstrate the importance of assessing the joint impact of climate indices across the monthly rainfall distribution, providing more complete inference than mean-based or single-index analyses.

Biography

Dr Dilani Kaveendri is a Lecturer at Canterbury Institute of Management, Sydney, and a recent PhD graduate from the University of Sydney. Her research focuses on Bayesian statistics, variable selection, quantile regression, spatial modelling, climate applications, and applied data science.

heritable: An R package for flexible heritability estimation from complex linear mixed models
Emi Tanaka
Abstract

Heritability is ubiquitous in quantitative genetics, yet its estimation and interpretation in more complex experimental settings like multi-environment trials remain challenging. We present heritable, an R package that implements multiple generalised heritability estimators within a unified framework. Our package supports five methods (Cullis, Delta, Oakey, Piepho, Standard) for computing broad-sense and narrow-sense heritabilities directly from model objects from commonly used mixed-modelling software, including lme4 and asreml. By fitting a single genotype-by-environment model, users can flexibly obtain heritability estimates for the main genotypic effect, the marginal genotypic effect across environments, or stratified genotypic effects within user-defined environmental strata. Our package also provides confidence intervals, visual and tabular summaries to aid interpretation and reporting. Using a simulation study spanning a range of realistic experimental scenarios, we further offer practical recommendations on the choice of heritability measure under varying design complexities. Taken together, this work aims to improve the use, reproducibility, and interpretability of heritability in more biologically realistic settings.

Biography

Dr. Emi Tanaka is an academic statistician at the Australian National University (ANU) with a passion for data science and open-source software. She serves as Editor-in-Chief of the R Journal, leads the ANU team for the Analytics for the Australian Grains Industry Project, and is an Elected Member of the International Statistical Institute.

Kernel Propagation of Gradient Boosted Margins for Spatio-temporal Forecasting
Ethan Kane Waters
Abstract

Gradient boosted trees are widely used due to their flexibility, minimal parametric assumptions and ability to learn complex relationships. However, they assume observational independence, potentially overlooking informative spatio-temporal structures. Existing modelling approaches that can explicitly consider spatio-temporal autocorrelation are often computationally intensive, rely on restrictive parametric assumptions or suffer when predictors are collinear. We propose a post-hoc method that augments gradient boosted tree predictions by using a kernel to propagate raw margins to nearby future observations. Margins are updated as a weighted combination of the original margin and a normalised kernel-weighted average of non-negative neighbouring margins which is controlled by a mixing parameter. This yields estimates independent of neighbourhood density that are bounded by the original prediction and the local neighbourhood. The method does not modify model training and is compatible with any gradient boosting implementation that exposes raw margins. Empirical results from the motivating biosecurity forecasting task of invasive species presence demonstrate consistent improvements in predictive performance over standard gradient boosting models.

Biography

Ethan Waters is a Data Scientist at the Department of Primary Industries, where he develops machine learning algorithms and statistical models to support data-driven decision-making in agriculture. Concurrently, Ethan is a full-time PhD student at QUT under the supervision of D/Prof Kerrie Mengersen, Prof Kate Helmstedt, Dr Ky Mathews, and Dr Mahdi Abolghasemi.

A Bayesian spatio-temporal nearest neighbor Gaussian process model for pooled genetic data
Imke Botha
Abstract

Large scale genetic datasets often aggregate the total allele counts of distinct genetic markers. Inferring haplotype frequencies (i.e. the frequency of multimarker alleles) from these pooled data is a challenge. Previous spatio-temporal modeling in this context has been limited to 3 markers due to the computational cost. In this work, we propose a nearest neighbor Gaussian process (NNGP) model to improve scaling with the number of markers and observations. To infer the parameters of our model, we develop a novel sequential Monte Carlo squared algorithm, which uses particle Gibbs with ancestor sampling to mutate the NNGP function values. The latter has a linear cost in the number of observations and the number of NNGPs, and can be applied to a broad range of NNGP models. As a case study, we analyze genetic data relating to antimalarial drug resistance in Africa, and show our scaling results empirically on a 3 and 6 genetic marker dataset.

Biography

Dr Imke Botha is a Research Fellow in the School of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Melbourne. Her background is in computational Bayesian statistics, and she is currently working on modelling and predicting the spread of antimalarial drug resistance in Asia. Her other research interests include sequential Monte Carlo, pseudo-marginal methods, and ensemble Kalman inversion methods.

Bespoke workshops to empower Agricultural Research Scientists to perform their own routine statistics
Kerry Bell
Abstract

The demand for statistical collaboration in agricultural research projects in the grains industry conducted within Queensland’s Department of Primary Industries (DPI) exceeds the capacity of the biometricians. Empowering researchers to perform routine statistical tasks offers a dual benefit: maintaining the quality of statistical practices in projects while enabling biometricians to focus on advanced methodologies, innovative statistical approaches, and strategic upskilling initiatives. Although the DPI biometry group has implemented various upskilling activities, these have not consistently translated into meaningful practice changes within research projects. To address this, tailored workshops designed around specific project groups have been trialled to bridge the gap between statistical training and practical application. Participants collaborate with biometricians to define learning objectives, explore statistical concepts using their own project data, and develop actionable plans to integrate these learnings into their research workflows. Preliminary feedback from participants indicates that these workshops have improved their confidence in data management and the use of statistics, leading to increased robustness in research outcomes. Additionally, the workshops have facilitated stronger collaboration between researchers and biometricians, creating a foundation for ongoing knowledge exchange and capacity building. This poster will provide an overview of the workshop design process, including the identification of key learning objectives, the integration of project-specific data, and the strategies employed to encourage practice change. The findings highlight the potential of tailored training initiatives to address capacity challenges and ensure the sustainability of high-quality statistical practices in agricultural research.

Biography

Kerry Bell is a Principal Biometrician at Queensland’s Department of Primary Industries in Toowoomba, where she leads the Applied Statistics group. With over 30 years’ experience in design, data management, analysis and reporting, she supports research in the grains and cotton industries and specialises in upskilling researchers in statistics using adult learning principles and facilitation tools.

Fusarium What? A method to identify mungbean lines and parents resistant and tolerant to Fusarium wilt
Lucas Peitton
Abstract

Fusarium wilt in mungbean is caused by fungi within the Fusarium oxysporum and F. solani species complexes and heavily affects grain production in Australia. The need for lines with high yield potential that can either retain yield in the presence of disease or tolerate the effects of the pathogen is imperative. Current selection methods involve the study of disease incidence and grain yield separately, which may result in not using all the available information and thus lead to inefficient selection decisions. A statistical model is presented where geneotypic resistance and tolerance measures are simultaneously derived from a multivariate linear mixed model analysis on grain yield and disease incidence for Mungbean under normal (uninoculated) circumstances and disease pressure (inoculated). The method incorporates genetic relatedness via pedigree information and is implemented in the ASReml-R package. A visual tool will be highlighted that identifies lines with higher yield potential, yield retention under disease pressure and tolerance to disease in the evaluated environment simultaneously. It has been demonstrated that resistance and tolerance proxies obtained from the genetic effects are independent of grain yield potential and disease incidence, allowing for more efficient selection decisions. As the genetic effects can be partitioned into additive and non-additive components, not only can improved lines be detected, but it is also possible to select potential parents for future crosses. These results are key in developing lines with better performance under disease pressure to ensure yield production for growers with or without the presence of the pathogen.

Biography

Lucas Peitton is a biometrician that works for the Queensland Department of Primary Industries through the Analytics for the Australian Grain Industry iniative funded by the Grains Research & Development Corporation. He has a Bachelor of Science with Major in Statistics from the National University of Rosario, Argentina. His interests are mainly related to quantitative genetics and R coding.

Estimating volcanic eruption recurrence rates using hierarchical trend renewal processes
Mark Bebbington
Abstract

Long-term (during quiescence) forecasts of volcanic eruptions are vital in estimating risk for land-use planning, but are challenging due to the typically sparse and incomplete data available in geological and/or historical eruption records. The typical solutions is to include in the analysis volcanoes with comparable physical properties and statistical behaviour (whatever these mean) to a target volcano. Analogue volcano recurrence patterns are thus used to estimate model parameters and forecast future eruptions. This approach often fails to consider the specific problem of “missing data”, which is common due to the uncertain and possibly unknowable processes in geologic records over thousands to tens of thousands of years. At a finer level, volcanoes can exhibit waxing, waning or cyclic activity in the rate of eruption onsets. This latter variability can be modelled using the trend renewal process using combinations of power, exponential and sine functions. On 14 example volcanoes, cases of constant activity level, increasing trend, wax and wane of activity, and cyclic plus trend behaviours are all observed. We propose using a set of hierarchical trend renewal processes to model analogue volcanoes and account for missing data. From these we create a Bayesian model averaging scheme for forecasting which incorporates model uncertainty by combining the posterior distribution of the forecast times from each of the considered models. We apply this method to forecasting eruptions from Mt Taranaki in New Zealand, which last erupted in ∼1780 AD and has its entire eruption record preserved only in geological deposits.

Biography

Mark Bebbington has a BSc (geophysics) and an MSc (probability) from VUW, and a PhD (applied probability) from Cambridge. After a post-doc at Queensland he took up a lectureship in statistics at Massey, and is now Professor in Geostatistics. Originally a statistical seismologist, Mark gravitated to volcanology and has focussed on developing new probabilistic techniques for eruption forecasting.

Fast Approximate MM-Estimation for Outlier Robust Model Selection
Martin Huang
Abstract

Stratified robust model selection reduces the impact of large residuals and overrepresented outliers in bootstrap samples but is computationally intensive when fitting iteratively-solved robust estimators across many candidate models. We propose FAMM, a Fast Approximate MM-estimator, implemented as a weighted least squares fit with weights derived from a full-data MM-estimator, to reduce this computational cost. Substituting the MM-estimator with FAMM preserves model selection performance while achieving a substantial speedup in typical dataset settings. We also demonstrate that FAMM satisfies the required conditions for model selection consistency.

Biography

Martin Huang is a third year PhD student at the University of Sydney, supervised by Associate Professor Garth Tarr and Professor Samuel Muller.

A forecasting disaster using sparce, scarce, and sporadic data to forecast a (mainly) unobservable nonlinear system
Melody Whitehead
Abstract

Forecasts of complex natural systems are required to inform decisions from emergency management to climate response. Forecasting methods rely on interpreting current knowledge and data and extrapolating the result into the future with causal and temporal assumptions.

For volcanic eruption forecasts, where the geological non-linear system operates over thousands to millions of years, the temporal-recency bias of instrumental data forces assumptions like time homogeneity (stationarity). These are significant limitations given that forecasts are intrinsically time-dependent, and system dynamics control future events.

In an attempt to sidestep these assumptions, we take a more holistic approach, using data and knowledge that are not commonly employed for volcano forecasting, thus expanding our available pool of information, but also expanding our catalogue of data and knowledge problems.

Here, we use the exemplar of Ruapehu volcano and the Central Volcanic Plateau in Aotearoa - New Zealand, to demonstrate methods with which we have tried and failed with, in the hope that this will inspire fruitful discussions on things that might be less ineffectual.

Biography

Geostatistican with a current focus on data, knowledge, and assumption limitations in natural hazards / volcanological modelling

ecreml: An R-package to incorporate environmental covariates into a multi-environment trial analysis
Michael Mumford
Abstract

A statistical methodology proposed in Mumford et al. (2023) integrates environmental covariates (ECs) into the multi-environment trial (MET) analysis with the aim of identifying environment drivers of genotype by environment by management practice (G×E×M) interaction effects. The methodology selects important ECs by incorporating them into a linear mixed model (LMM) with complex variance structures using ASReml-R. The selection procedure can be used to enhance the prediction of the performance of treatments and/or genotypes under untested environmental conditions. One difficulty arising from the proposed methodology is that the R-code to setup the selection procedure algorithm in conjunction with fitting the LMM is complicated, potentially creating a barrier to applying the methodology to other datasets.

This presentation outlines the recent development of an R-package called ecreml to compliment the Mumford et al. (2023) methodology. The ecreml R-package automates the iterative selection procedure which involves identifying important ECs via \(k\)-fold cross-validation and incorporating them into the LMM using forward selection. Once EC terms are included in the LMM, non-significant EC terms are removed using backwards selection procedures. The R-package can easily be installed via GitHub (https://github.com/michaelhm-daf/ecreml) and includes a vignette demonstrating the functionality of the ecreml R-package when applied to a motivating MET sorghum dataset.

The ecreml R-package enables statisticians and agricultural scientists to easily analyse their own MET data using the methodology of Mumford et al. (2023) to identify key ECs contributing to G×E×M interaction effect.

Biography

Michael is currently employed as a biometrician at the Queensland Department of Primary Industries in Toowoomba, Australia. Michael works across numerous crop science projects, focusing on the design and analysis of agricultural experiments. Michael is also completing PhD studies part-time, researching improved statistical methodologies for the analysis of comparative scientific experiments.

Unconditioning Fisher’s Exact Test
Mst Bithi Akter
Abstract

The Analysis of 2 × 2 contingency tables remain one of the oldest problems in statistics, and it is still very much with us today. Fisher’s exact test is popular for its reliable type I error control, but it is known to be conservative, with its actual significance level often lower than the intended level. This can cause a noticeable loss of statistical power, especially when sample sizes are small.

The exact unconditional test has become much more popular in recent decades, due to increasing computing power and availability of statistical software. Still, its conservatism is a major issue, especially when working with different sampling designs. In this study, we propose a novel method that addresses the conservativeness of the unconditional exact test in both one-fixed-margin and no-fixed-margin designs.

We look at three common sampling frameworks in this study: two fixed margins, one fixed margin, and no fixed margins. Using recent advances in binomial and multinomial sampling models, we systematically compare our method to existing exact and unconditional tests. We focus on type I error control, power, and robustness across a wide range of parameter settings.

Our approach offers a good balance between type I error and higher power. By reducing conservativeness in both fixed-margin and no-fixed-margin designs, this work helps develop more efficient exact methods for analyzing small and moderate samples. The study also highlights the ongoing need to revisit classic problems in contingency table analysis with modern computational and methodological tools.

Biography

Mst Bithi Akter is a PhD student in Statistics at the School of Mathematics and Statistics, UNSW Sydney. My research focuses on Statistical Inference, Discrete Copula models, discrete data analysis and model development and statistical methodology for discrete outcomes.

Quasi-posteriors for robust adaptive clinical trial design with count outcomes
Navodya Abirami Naotunna Gamacharige
Abstract

Modern clinical trials are often designed within a Bayesian framework using trial simulation. This requires specifying assumptions for data generation including a treatment effect and a distribution for the data. Often the performance of the design depends on such assumptions meaning that if they are misspecified, then it could lead to the design performing worse than expected. To address this limitation for clinical trials where count outcomes are observed, we propose to develop designs within a general Bayesian inference framework. This enables replacing the likelihood in standard Bayesian inference with the quasi-likelihood to form a quasi-posterior. This results in inference being largely based on assumptions about the mean and variance model for the data. We propose to leverage such a property to design adaptive trials that are robust across a range of potential data generating models. Such an approach is evaluated through the re-design of a recently conducted clinical trial to assess the performance of citalopram (20 mg and 40 mg) in reducing cocaine use. A range of scenarios are considered including equidispersed, overdispersed, and underdispersed data where we compare our approach to standard practice within trial simulation. The results suggest that a design approach based on the quasi-likelihood instils robustness into the trial design and offers a potential solution to a major limitation in trial design.

Biography

Naotunna Gamacharige Navodya Abirami is a PhD candidate in the School of Mathematical Sciences and a member of the Centre for Data Science at Queensland University of Technology, where her research proposes robust methods for designing Bayesian adaptive clinical trials. She holds a BSc Honours in Industrial Statistics from the University of Colombo, Sri Lanka.

Fitting Generalised Linear Mixed Models using Sequential Quadratic Programming
Peter Green
Abstract

Finding maximum likelihood estimates in generalised linear mixed models (GLMMs) can be difficult due to the often-intractable integral over the random effects. Ensuring convergence can be tricky, especially in binomial GLMMs, and often multiple optimisers and settings need to be tried to get satisfactory results. This is exacerbated if you want to use parametric bootstrap for your inference. Sequential quadratic programming (SQP) is a method for solving optimisation problems with nonlinear constraints. SQP offers an alternative option for maximising the Laplace approximation to the GLMM likelihood, bypassing the need for an inner penalised iterative reweighted least squares (PIRLS) loop. This talk discusses the implementation of SQP for GLMMs and compares its performance to other common approaches.

Biography

Peter Green is a research statistician at Tadorna Data Science.

A Bayesian predictive density for Type II censored data for a normal distribution
Takeshi Kurosawa
Abstract

We discuss predictive densities for Type II censored data. Type II censoring can be viewed as a problem of order statistics. For example, a fixed number of batteries is prepared, and some of the batteries run out over time. We aim to predict the time until the next battery runs out, which can be formulated as a Type-II censoring problem. We apply this method to failure-time data from aircraft air-conditioning equipment as an illustrative example. We evaluate predictive densities in terms of the risk based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence. We derive a new Bayesian predictive density for unobserved data under censoring. The derived predictive density has the minimax property within a class of scale-invariant families. In this study, we focus on the Type-II censoring problem for order statistics from normal distributions. We show that the predictive density can be expressed as a truncated t-distribution. As a benchmark, we consider the plug-in predictive density, obtained by substituting the maximum likelihood estimates into the unknown parameters of the true distribution. The plug-in predictive density also belongs to the scale-invariant family under the assumed setting. Therefore, we demonstrate that the proposed predictive density is superior to the plug-in predictive density in terms of risk under the Kullback-Leibler divergence, owing to its minimax property. Furthermore, we conduct simulation studies to demonstrate the validity of the proposed predictive density for predicting unobserved data under censoring.

Biography

Takeshi Kurosawa (TK) is a member of the Department of Applied Mathematics at Tokyo University of Science in Japan. TK is a professor of mathematical statistics in the department. TK’s research areas are generalized linear models, errors-in-variables models. Gao Xin (GX) was a master’s student and conducted research under TK’s supervision. GX studied Bayesian decision theory while at university.

Analysing longitudinal opioid dispensing patterns among injured patients using sequential mixture hidden Markov models
Tasmiah Sad Sutopa
Abstract

Pain management following injury can be complex, and may involve prescription medications, particularly opioids. Prolonged opioid use is known to increase risk of mental and physical harms. Although many studies have explored individual-level factors associated with cross-sectional opioid use, less is known about opioid dispensing states over time. The main aim of this study is to identify and analyse community opioid dispensing patterns among injured patients. The study used a linked dataset comprising hospital admissions, community pharmaceutical opioid dispensing and mortality information for Queensland adults hospitalised due to injury between 2014 to 2015 and dispensed opioids at least once during 2-years of follow-up. We calculated weekly opioid morphine equivalents (OMEs) by aggregating the daily dispensing quantity for seven days. Weekly opioid exposure was categorised into three states: no opioid use, low opioid use (<50 OME), and high opioid use (50+ OME). Sequential Mixture Hidden Markov Models were used to identify groups based on the transition of dispensing states over time. We then applied multinomial logistic regression to explore the association between patient characteristics and group membership. Among 50,152 injured patients, five opioid trajectory groups were identified: Persistent high (3.2%), Persistent low (13.1%), Minimal (39.4%), Intermittent (11.2%), and Persistent no opioid dispensing (33.1%). Compared to patients with no subsequent hospitalisation, those with 5+ encounters had a much higher relative risk (RR: 7.07-13.69) of being in any opioid dispensing group than Persistent no opioid dispensing group. Intensive care unit admission and pre-injury opioid dependence were associated with Persistent high and Intermittent dispensing. Repeated hospitalisation, older age and pre-injury opioid dependence were associated with group membership. The study provides novel evidence on long-term opioid prescription trajectories among injured patients.

Biography

Tasmiah Sad Sutopa is a PhD candidate at Queensland University of Technology. Her PhD focuses on using better statistical methods in longitudinal pharmaceutical opioid dispensing among injured patients. She is also a faculty member in Department of Statistics, University of Dhaka, Bangladesh. She holds Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in Statistics, and she has published 8 journal articles.

A minimal extension of the Bradley-Terry model for paired comparisons with cyclic dominance
Yuki Ohno
Abstract

Paired comparison data arise in a wide range of fields, such as sports analysis, social choice, and machine learning. The Bradley-Terry model is a well-established mathematical model for estimating latent rankings of items based on such data. It imposes a probabilistic transitivity constraint under which each pairwise preference is required to be consistent with a global ranking, and this constraint contributes to excellent performance in many applications. However, empirical data sometimes exhibit cyclic dominance, resembling dynamics like “rock-paper-scissors”, which may violate the transitivity assumption underlying this classical framework. In such cases, analyses based on this framework may lead to misleading inferences. Instead, we seek to quantify the extent of cyclic dominance in order to assess the degree of departure from transitivity. To this end, we propose a minimal extension of the Bradley-Terry model by introducing only a single nonnegative parameter. When this additional parameter is set to zero, the proposed model reduces to the Bradley-Terry model. It also provides a simple and interpretable measure of departure from the Bradley-Terry model in terms of transitivity. The usefulness of the proposed model is demonstrated through the analysis of real data, where it successfully captures cyclic dominance.

Biography

Yuki Ohno is a second-year master’s student at Tokyo University of Science and plans to pursue a Ph.D. His research interests include categorical data analysis, particularly the analysis of contingency tables with missing data.

High-throughput phenotyping models predict wheat yield across current and future climates
Zixiong Zhaung
Abstract

Future climate change includes both elevated CO\(_2\) and warming, both climate factors could significantly influence photosynthesis and global wheat production, one of the major crops for food security1. However, few studies have addressed the combined effects of elevated CO\(_2\) and warming (Ainsworth and Long, 2021). Breeding and selecting wheat that adapt to future climate change requires efficiently evaluating thousands of varieties across both current and future growing conditions. To address challenges at this scale, high-throughput phenotyping technologies offer a novel path to breed better crops for future climates. However, their value for predicting yield under novel climates remains untested. Over two years I grew 86 diverse Australian wheat lines under current and projected end-of-century conditions (800 ppm CO\(_2\), +5 °C), phenotyping each with 3D multispectral scanning, digital microscope, hyperspectral leaf-clip reflectance, and a wheat-specific deep-learning model that predicts leaf photosynthetic physiology (Furbank et al. 2021). Over the two years of experiments, future conditions consistently reduced grain yield by 17 ± 2%. This further emphasises the needs to breed wheat varieties better adapted to future climate conditions. From over 140 high-throughput traits ~30 features were selected using elastic net and ablation studies and was able to predict wheat yield with an \(R^2\) of 0.62 using recently published in-context learning foundational models4. Additionally, this model could predict the yield of unseen genotypes with no loss of accuracy (\(R^2\) = 0.60), which is needed to screen new breeding lines. This result demonstrates that predictive models using scalable, sensor-derived phenotypes mutual across growth environments rather than being environment-specific may be feasible. Additionally, predictive models using phenotyping-based approaches also offer mechanistic insights of adaptation strategies across environments. This further enhances the confidence for breeding and pre-breeding exercises for addressing food security issues driven by climate change.

Keynote #3 - Prof. Margarita Moreno-Betancur
Chair: David Reid
Details
Causal inference in health research
Prof. Margarita Moreno-Betancur
Abstract

The ultimate goal of medical and health research is to improve patient outcomes and population health. As a result, an overwhelming majority of clinical and public health research studies ask “causal” questions, concerning the effect of treatments, policies, behaviours and other exposures on health outcomes, even if often unadmitted. In many cases, especially in the current era of data deluge, these studies rely on observational (non-experimental) data to address causal questions. Unfortunately, for a long time the statistics discipline largely shunned the possibility of causal inference beyond randomised trials, and instead focused on the development of tools such as regression models without clarity regarding their usefulness and limitations for addressing the causal questions that substantive areas continued to ask. In recent decades, however, the discipline has seen the rise of a new area focused on determining the settings and approaches that could allow causal inference from observational data. This talk will first provide an overview of some of the fundamental contributions of this statistical area to enable and improve the study of causality in health research and then provide an overview of recent advances in the area seeking further to advance the statistical methods, teaching and practice.

Biography

Professor Margarita Moreno-Betancur is co-Director of the Clinical Epidemiology and Biostatistics Unit at the Melbourne Children’s campus. She established an internationally recognised hub of innovation and expertise in statistical methods for observational studies, supported by competitive fellowship and grant funding. Her team conducts methodological research in causal inference and missing data while contributing their expertise to health research studies. She is Chair of the Victorian Centre for Biostatistics leadership team, Scientific Lead of the LifeCourse platform of cohort studies, and Editor of the journal Epidemiology. She was awarded the Moran Medal by the Australian Academy of Science in 2025.
