Dynamic risk prediction of ICU discharge alive using longitudinal urea-to-creatinine measurements
Sophie Zaloumis
Abstract

Up to 6 million intensive care unit (ICU) patients worldwide develop ICU acquired weakness (ICU AW) annually. ICU AW is linked to mortality and long term reductions in health related quality of life. Early physical rehabilitation in ICU may improve strength, but identifying patients who could benefit from early rehabilitation and knowing when early rehabilitation should occur are uncertain. Identifying real-time patient biomarkers related to rehabilitation outcomes could help inform these decisions. We assessed the urea to creatinine ratio (UCR) as a real time biomarker of catabolism to guide rehabilitation. A dynamic prediction model used joint modelling: a longitudinal submodel for log2(UCR) (linear mixed effects with natural cubic splines) and a Cox survival submodel for discharge alive, linked by current value and slope. The joint model was fitted with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo via stan_jm (rstanarm R package). Performance was evaluated by calibration, dynamic area under the curve (AUC) and patient level predictions. In 180 patients (167 discharged alive, 13 died), a doubling of UCR (for the same trajectory slope) was associated with a 0.82 fold (95% credible interval (CI) 0.62–1.08) reduction in the hazard of ICU discharge alive. For the same current UCR level, a one unit increase in the current slope of log2(UCR) trajectory was associated with a 0.23 (95% CI 0.06–0.90) reduction in the hazard of ICU discharge alive. The longitudinal model fit well; survival probabilities were sensitive to UCR changes. Higher and rising UCR predicted higher probability of remaining in ICU. Calibration was reasonable in the training and test datasets; dynamic AUCs were unstable in the small test set (n=36). Results suggest UCR may help dynamically predict outcomes to inform rehabilitation decisions.

Biography

Sophie Zaloumis is a Biostatistician and Senior Research Fellow at the University of Melbourne (BSc Hons 2006; PhD 2011). She has over 10 years’ experience leading and collaborating in public-health research. Her research interests focus on applications of statistical methodology for handling complex biological and real-time data, particularly for the purpose of prediction modelling.

How Are Researchers Using MIMIC? A Methods-Focused Review of Studies in Critical Care
Tayyebeh Kenarangi
Abstract

The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) database is a widely used open data resource in critical care research. Its accessibility has led to large numbers of research studies being published; however, there are concerns about the comparability and reproducibility of studies due to variation in design and analysis decisions and how they are reported. Methods: We reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 that used the MIMIC database. A random sample of 100 eligible studies was identified through the OpenAlex bibliographic database and assessed using a structured extraction framework. Information was extracted on study aims, cohort definitions, exclusion criteria, outcome specification, handling of missing data, and analytical methods. The review focused on how key design and analytical decisions were reported and justified. Results: Studies reported findings from general ICU and specific clinical populations; the study population could not be determined for 30 of the 100 studies. Predictive modelling was the most common study design (\(n\) = 60), but only one study included external validation. Core methodological decisions were frequently underreported or inconsistently justified, including length‑of‑stay thresholds, age criteria, and mortality time horizons. Handling of missing data was not reported in more than half of studies (\(n\) = 56), despite missing data being common in MIMIC. Conclusions: MIMIC‑based studies demonstrate considerable variation in study and analysis that are not always transparently reported. Improved reporting of design and analytical decisions is needed to strengthen the validity, reproducibility, and generalisability of registry‑based critical care research.

Biography

Tayyebeh is a PhD student in public health at QUT.

11:00-11:15
A geostatistical framework for spatial sampling design and data integration in on-farm experimentation
Zhanglong Cao
Abstract

On-farm experimentation (OFE) increasingly generates rich spatial datasets, including high-resolution yield maps, proximal sensing surveys, remote-sensing products, and sparse point-source laboratory measurements such as soil cores and tissue tests. However, statistical guidance on how to design cost-effective spatial sampling strategies and integrate these heterogeneous data sources when estimating treatment effects remains limited. This study presents a geostatistical framework addressing three practical questions encountered in large-scale field experiments. First, how densely should point-source measurements be collected? We derive sampling intervals from the variogram range via the kriging equations, and show by Monte Carlo simulation that a multi-scale nested reconnaissance design of roughly one hundred points recovers the spatial structure needed to calibrate the main sampling campaign more reliably than grid or random designs of the same size. Second, how many field cores should be combined within a composite sample? We derive an optimal compositing rule that balances laboratory cost, field cost, and the nugget-to-sill ratio, reducing sampling variance with minimal information loss. Third, how should sparse point samples be integrated with dense spatial covariates? Comparing a kriged-covariate approach against a joint bivariate spatial mixed model, simulation shows that integration can materially improve treatment-effect estimation, with benefits governed by point-sample density and, for the joint model, whether the cross-layer spatial covariance is estimable. We characterise when each approach is preferable, and when neither improves on the dense data alone.

Biography

Dr Zhanglong Cao is a Lecturer in Statistics at EECMS, Curtin University. His research focuses on statistical modelling, Bayesian methods, on-farm experimentation, precision agriculture, and applied data science. He works closely with industry and research partners to develop data-driven solutions for agricultural decision-making.

11:15-11:30
ST-MICE: A Trajectory-Aware Multiple Imputation Framework for Spatial Coordinates and Associated Variables
Amuchechukwu Ibenegbu
Abstract

Spatiotemporal trajectory datasets are central to environmental and scientific applications such as tropical cyclone monitoring, ocean circulation analysis and movement ecology. They contain ordered geographic coordinates and associated physical or environmental variables, but are often incomplete due to sensor failure, communication gaps, irregular sampling and quality-control filtering. A key challenge is that the coordinates defining where an observation belongs may be missing, while variables measured or associated with that location may also be absent. Standard imputation methods are not fully suited to this setting because they often ignore nonlinear trajectory geometry or assume that coordinates are fully observed. We propose ST-MICE, a trajectory-aware multiple imputation framework for imputing missing coordinates and associated spatiotemporal variables. ST-MICE represents each trajectory using a principal curve and derives a normalised arc-length parameter that captures geometric progression along the path. This representation guides coordinate interpolation and serves as a geometry-aware predictor within a chained-equation framework for refining associated variables. By combining coordinate reconstruction with multivariate refinement, ST-MICE preserves trajectory structure while exploiting dependencies among coordinates and variables. The method is evaluated on publicly available environmental trajectory datasets, including tropical cyclone tracks and ocean surface drifter paths, under missing completely at random (MCAR) and missing at random (MAR) mechanisms, and is compared with several baselines. Results show that ST-MICE achieves competitive and often superior performance, especially for nonlinear trajectories and for simultaneous missingness in coordinates and associated variables.

Biography

Amuchechukwu Ibenegbu is a PhD candidate in Statistics at UNSW Sydney, supervised by A/Prof Rohitash Chandra and A/Prof Pierre Lafaye de Micheaux. Her research focuses on spatiotemporal statistical modelling, missing-data imputation and machine learning, with current work on ST-MICE, a trajectory-aware multiple imputation framework for environmental trajectory data.

11:30-11:45
Tools for Causal Interpretation
Chris Howden
Abstract

Causality is becoming the new buzz word. Everywhere you look there are causal workshops and talks, some journals are even encouraging authors to use Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG’s). Researchers across disciplines are asking how they can move beyond reporting associations to making credible causal claims. In this talk I will discuss when we should be aiming for causality instead of correlation and suggest a practical workflow for causal inference applicable across most domains. Some of the more common tools for causal interpretation will be discussed such as randomisation & Target Trials along with how we might classify them into different types of tools – each with different advantages, limitations, assumptions and tricks for implementation. An important distinction will be made between “objective” causal tools that work largely irrelevant to the users experience e.g. randomisation, versus “subjective” tools that require experience and skill to use effectively e.g. DAG’s and Target Trials. Understanding these pros, cons, assumptions and differences will help researchers select the appropriate tools for making stronger, more defensible causal claims.

Biography

Chris leads the Statistical Consulting Unit at Sydney University. We elevate the university’s impact and statistical practice by upskilling researchers to carry out best practice, high-impact analyses and optimally designed studies. He has been teaching and applying advanced statistical methods since 1999, managing statistical teams since 2006 and owned a data science company for over a decade.

Parsimonious modelling of unstructured and structured random-effect covariance in glmmTMB
Maeve McGillycuddy
Abstract

Generalised linear mixed models provide a framework for modelling dependent data. Many applications require multiple covariance structures to account for different sources of correlation; however, finding a single open-source modelling tool capable of fitting these structures can be challenging. We present two new covariance structures in the R package glmmTMB that broaden the range of models that can be fitted while retaining the package’s familiar syntax. The first method introduces reduced-rank covariance structures for high-dimensional random effects. This approach parsimoniously approximates a covariance matrix using latent variables. The second method introduces a proportional covariance structure, allowing users to specify random effects whose covariance matrix is proportional to a known covariance matrix. This has a range of applications, including phylogenetically and pedigree structured random effects, and spline smoothers defined through basis functions. Together, these methods allow users to combine latent variables, structured random effects, smoothers, and other mixed-model terms within a single modelling framework. We illustrate their applications using ecological and plant breeding examples, demonstrating models that were previously difficult or impossible to fit using existing software.

Biography

Maeve is a statistical consultant at UNSW Sydney. Their research focuses on developing statistical methods for structured data, including mixed models, covariance structures, and multivariate methods, with applications in ecology.

12:00-12:15
Feature selection in censored-covariate regression models
Rajan Shankar
Abstract

Censored-covariate regression models arise when a response variable is modelled using a covariate that is only partially observed due to censoring. Existing methods for fitting these models focus on parameter estimation, and do not directly address the problem of selecting features that may affect the response variable, the censored covariate, or both. We propose a penalised likelihood method that jointly models the response variable and a single right-censored covariate, and applies separate \(L_1\) penalties to the feature coefficients in the two model components. Parameters are estimated using an Expectation-Minimisation (EM) algorithm, where the minimisation step separates into two optimisation problems corresponding to the response-variable and censored-covariate model components. A simulation study shows that the method can recover distinct sets of active features for the two model components under adequate signal. We apply our method to Huntington disease (HD) data from the PREDICT-HD study, using cognitive ability measured by the Symbol Digit Modalities Test score as the response variable and time-to-diagnosis of HD as the right-censored covariate, and using brain region volumes as features. The selected features suggest partly distinct brain-region profiles for cognitive ability and time-to-diagnosis, including basal-ganglia regions in the time-to-diagnosis model component. A stability analysis shows that the HD data contains weak signal, clarifying the extent to which the selected features should be trusted.

Biography

I am a final-year statistics PhD candidate at the University of Sydney. My broad research interest is in regularised methods for modelling complex data, where I am specifically interested in feature selection, constrained optimisation, outlier detection, and robust statistics.

12:15-12:30
Model-based Assessment of Functional and Phylogenetic Diversity
Shaoqian Huang
Abstract

Biodiversity is a quantity of fundamental interest, yet its measurement remains challenging. Two key aspects of biodiversity are functional diversity (FD) and phylogenetic diversity (PD).

Commonly used distance-based diversity measures are typically affected by sampling intensity. Moreover, there is currently no established statistical framework for analyzing how diversity varies along environmental gradients.

Here, we propose a model-based approach to assessing PD and FD that is robust to variation in sampling intensity and enables the study of diversity changes along environmental gradients.

By reparameterizing abundance models, we decompose variation in abundance into components associated with total abundance (alpha-diversity) and relative abundance (beta-diversity). Simulation results further indicate that changes in PD and FD arise when the beta-diversity coefficients are aligned with the principal axes of the phylogenetic or functional similarity matrix, which can be interpreted as linear contrasts of the beta-diversity coefficients. In addition, we develop a biplot by projecting the compositional effects of each observation, providing a visualization of how diversity differentiates across gradient levels in a percentage cover dataset.

Overall, this framework integrates the measurement of PD and FD changes along environmental gradients into a model-based setting, offering improved interpretability, flexibility, and computational efficiency.

Biography

Shaoqian Huang is a PhD candidate in the School of Mathematics and Statistics at UNSW Sydney. His research focuses on joint species modelling and its applications to biodiversity quantification. He is particularly interested in developing statistical methods for measuring phylogenetic and functional diversity. He has also worked on ecological niche modelling using probabilistic approaches.

Bayesian or machine learning approaches: what works best for genomic prediction?
Prof. Ben Hayes
Abstract

The foundational paper for genomic prediction, predicting complex traits from genome wide DNA markers, was published in 2001. Since then, genomic prediction has been widely adopted in crop and livestock production, and in human genetics for prediction of disease risk. In this overview, statistical methodologies for genomic prediction are compared, and we then speculate on the future of genomic prediction methodologies.

AI-Integrated Genomic Prediction Framework for Parent Selection in Australian Macadamia Germplasm
Lin, Ni-Jung
Abstract

Macadamia, an Australian native subtropical perennial tree crop, presents critical breeding challenges due to inherent heterogeneity, long juvenility, single plant basis progeny evaluation, and the complex genotype by environment interactions. Aiming to develop and validate an efficient parent selection framework by integrating advanced statistical methods, genomic tools and artificial intelligence (AI). Phenotypic yield data of 10,156 individuals across ten trials in Queensland and New South Wales since the 1990s. Genomic comprehensive analysis included 2,010 accessions across four species (Macadamia integrifolia, M. tetraphylla, M. ternifolia, and M. jansenii) that were genotyped by 12,655 DArT markers, revealing 45.45% missing marker rate. Informative markers were filtered by call rate at 90% and minor allele frequency at 1%, remaining 1,931 markers. Three imputation algorithms: (1) mode, (2) k-nearest neighbors (KNNi), and (3) random forest (missForest), implemented in R. Imputation accuracy was assessed by randomly masking 5% of the data, 78.60%, 87.14%, and 84.73%, respectively. Population structure identified 2 to 4 genetic clusters explaining 17.45% to 20.05% of the total variation, with clear species differentiation and admixture in breeding germplasm. Estimate prediction through family variance for half-sib and full-sib accounted for 31.69% and 15.84% of the variation, respectively. Pedigree-based best linear unbiased prediction (ABLUP) estimated narrow-sense (h2) and broad-sense (H2) heritability at 25.29% and 39.20%, matching plot means (A*BLUP) estimates. An AI-integrated framework combining phenotypic analysis of multi-environment trials, linear genomic models, and non-linear approaches will be developed, including random forest, support vector machine, multilayer perceptron, and stacking ensemble learning. This framework has strong potential for shortening breeding cycles and accelerating genetic gain in macadamia breeding programs.

Biography

My name is LIN, NI-JUNG. I am a PhD student at the University of Queensland. My research topic is focusing on macadamia breeding. I am doing this through AI-based genomic prediction. My hope is that this research will accelerate genetic gain in macadamia breeding. So far, I have designed my experiment design and ran genomic data analysis.

Parameter Tuning in Statistics and Machine Learning Models for Plant Genetic Improvement Using Bayesian Optimization
Zitong Li
Abstract

Genomic prediction has become a central tool in modern plant and animal breeding, enabling early selection of superior candidates using genome-wide marker data. A wide range of high dimensional statistics and machine learning models have been applied in this context, including penalized regression, Bayesian regression, ensemble methods such as random forests, and deep learning. However, their predictive performance is highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices, and efficient tuning remains challenging due to high-dimensional, heterogeneous search spaces and limited computational budgets. Bayesian optimization provides a principled and sample-efficient framework for hyperparameter tuning in various machine learning models. Nevertheless, its effectiveness can vary across model classes and problem settings, and practical guidelines for its application in genomic prediction remain limited. In addition, hyperparameter tuning is typically formulated as a single-objective problem focused on predictive accuracy, despite the importance of model simplicity and interpretability in breeding applications. In this work, we present a systematic study of Bayesian optimization for genomic prediction across a diverse set of model classes. We evaluate its performance under different hyperparameter tuning scenarios and analyse how optimization behaviour varies across models and search spaces. We further investigate the impact of objective selection in hyperparameter tuning by comparing predictive performance-based criteria with model selection criteria, and explore a multi-objective formulation to balance accuracy and model parsimony. Our results provide practical insights into effective hyperparameter tuning strategies for genomic prediction, demonstrated on both simulated data and real cotton datasets.

Biography

Dr Zitong Li is a Senior research scientist in CSIRO. His research focuses on applied and computational statistics, with applications in genetics, genomics, and plant breeding.

Resource optimised designs: Determining variety replication status
David Hughes
Abstract

Early evaluation stages in plant breeding programs involve large numbers of test lines, grown in experiments in order to select the best. Widely used partially replicated designs of Cullis et al. (2006) have led to significant improvements in selection accuracy. In their design construction, Cullis et al. (2006) did not use information on the genetic relatedness of lines, due to the lack of suitable design software at the time. Cullis et al. (2020) used the ODW package to show that selection accuracy can be substantially improved with designs that incorporate genetic relatedness in the allocation of plots to test lines. This talk will present an additional step that uses genetic relatedness to determine an optimal subset of test lines to be replicated, subject to seed availability. Advantages of this approach are demonstrated to resource allocation using an in silico study based on an early stage selection experiment in chickpeas.

Biography

PhD Student at the University of Wollongong under the supervision of Prof. Brian Cullis and Dr Alison Smith. Biometrician with nearly 10 years of experience in agricultural research. Currently employed as a research scientist at Sugar Research Australia (SRA).

11:15-11:30
Estimating cell-type-specific gene co-expression and spatial autocorrelation for spot-level spatial transcriptomics data
Max Woollard
Abstract

Accurately estimating gene-gene co-expression is key to understanding biological processes. However, it is important to recognise the context of these gene-gene co-expressions. First, these co-expression structures can vary with different cell types, meaning we should expect the corresponding covariance matrices for different cell types to be different(1). Furthermore, gene expression activity varies across space with spatial autocorrelation, which must be taken into account to accurately estimate the covariance matrices(2). Spatial transcriptomics data addresses these challenges by measuring transcriptomic activity at many spots in a tissue, and these spots often contain a mixture of different cell types(3).

To this end, we propose CSSpatialNet, a statistical model to describe both cell-type-specific gene covariances and and cell-type-specific gene expressions’ spatial autocorrelations from spot-level spatial transcriptomics data. The parameters of the model are then estimated by maximising the likelihood of the observed spot-level data, which is computationally efficient using the standard gradient descent method.

Our simulation studies show CSSpatialNet provides more accurate estimation of the cell-type-specific covariance matrices than competing methods that either ignore cell-type or discard spatial information Additionally, CSSpatialNet estimates the spatial autocorrelation of each gene within each cell type. We are also evaluating our method on real spatial transcriptomics data at a range of resolutions, such as Visium Mouse Embryo data. By accounting for the varying levels of spatial autocorrelation among genes and cell types, we expect to see more accurate cell-type-specific gene co-expression estimates.

11:30-11:45
From Pixels to Phenotypes: Building Statistical Pipelines for Drone-Based Field Experiments
Colleen Hunt
Abstract

Early biomass measurement in sorghum is essential for assessing plant health at early developmental stages and identifying factors such as soil deficiencies or disease. Conventionally, biomass estimation relies on destructive sampling, which limits repeated measurements on the same plants and hinders longitudinal analysis of biomass accumulation. This limitation has historically impeded efforts to explain growth trajectories. In this study, destructive biomass measurements from a sorghum field trial were used as ground truth to develop predictive models estimating plant biomass from drone imagery. Calibration analysis was conducted to ensure precise measurement of early plant biomass via image analysis. The developed framework facilitated multiple biomass assessments throughout the growing season. The 2023 heterosis trial included 150 inbred lines and 457 hybrid crosses. Early biomass was predicted at two time points using both destructive weight measurements and estimates obtained from drone imagery. A multi-trait dynamic linear mixed model was applied to evaluate the accuracy of the image-based predictions. Results demonstrated a high correlation between destructive measurements and imaging estimates, indicating that biomass imaging for early sorghum biomass assessment is both reliable and effective.

Multi-trait multi-environment models enhances prediction and interpretation of grain yield in wheat field trials
Nick Fradgley
Abstract

Linear mixed models are widely used for analysis of genotype by environment interactions (GEI) in multi environment field trials (METs) for crop breeding. Well established methods employ factor analytic approximation of heterogeneous genetic covariance structures across environments to group environments into interaction classes (iClasses) that minimise cross-over interactions for single traits of interest (Smith et al., 2021). While grain yield is the main trait of interest for cereal crops such as wheat, multiple secondary traits, such as phenology, plant architecture and resistance to often unpredictably occurring diseases, are known to drive complex GEI effects for grain yield. Enhanced prediction of secondary adaptive traits may help improve prediction of grain yield GEI and enhance selection of well adapted genotypes.

Here, we extend the factor analytic linear mixed model framework for joint modelling of multiple secondary traits—including days to heading, plant height, and disease scores for Yellow (Stripe) rust and Fusarium crown rot—in addition to grain yield, to a multi-year MET as part of the CAIGE program (Trethowan et al., 2024). Accurate model fitting required partitioning genetic covariance among traits and environments, while separately accounting for correlated residual spatial trends among traits within environments. Secondary traits were generally more heritable than grain yield, exhibited stronger genetic correlations across environments, and showed higher proportions of additive genetic variance. Importantly, genetic correlations between secondary traits and grain yield varied markedly in both magnitude and direction across yield iClasses, reflecting their contrasting adaptive processes. This approach could be particularly useful when highly heritable secondary traits are assessed in earlier stages of a breeding program before multi-environment yield trials, thus allowing more accurate selection from a larger set of candidate genotypes.

Biography

Nick Fradgley is a GRDC-funded Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the University of Sydney. His research focuses on developing and applying quantitative genetics methods in cereal breeding. He completed his PhD at the University of Cambridge (2022) and held a postdoctoral position with CSIRO, Australia (2025).

Validity and interpretability of estimated effects from mixed model based meta-analysis
Khageswor Giri
Abstract

Mixed models are a commonly used method to undertake meta-analysis for synthesising evidence across different experiments/studies. Such analyses rely on a key implicit assumption that all contributing studies estimate the same underlying quantity on a comparable measurement scale. In this presentation, we use meta-analysis of data from individual dairy cow pasture dry matter intake (DMI) from a series of experiments to illustrate how violation of this assumption can affect the validity and interpretability of estimated effects.

Individual cow pasture DMI, estimated using the alkane method, was analysed across multiple controlled experiments using linear mixed models with experiment, cow and cow within experiment as random effects. Initial diagnostics of the fitted model revealed a pronounced temporal pattern in the estimated experiment effects: experiments conducted before 2021 tended to have negative effects, whereas those conducted after 2021 tended to have positive effects. The shift corresponded to an average difference of approximately 5 kg DMI per cow per day between earlier and later experiments, suggesting a systematic change that could not be readily attributed to biological factors alone.

Further investigation indicated that a refinement to the laboratory alkane estimation procedure occurred around the same period, providing a plausible explanation for the observed positive shift in estimated pasture DMI. We discuss diagnostic approaches for detecting such scale shifts, practical mitigation strategies for mixed-model based meta-analysis, and the broader implications for statisticians working with large, multi-study datasets where measurement/estimation protocols may evolve over time.

Biography

Khageswor Giri, Senior Biometrician, brings over 17 years of experience in applied statistics of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Ecology. His work is evidenced by the development and application of rigorous statistical methodologies that inform evidence-based decision-making, contributing to high-impact scientific research.

Keynote #5 - Associate Prof. Peter Dunn
Chair: Bethany Rognoni
Details
Modelling continuous data with exact zeros
Associate Prof. Peter Dunn
Abstract

Statistical models for continuous data (e.g., linear regression) and discrete data (e.g., logistic regression) are commonly used. Continuous data with exact zeros, while less common, appear in many applications. In this talk, different models are discussed for modelling this type of data, with a focus on using Poisson-gamma models, which are Poisson sums of gamma distributions. Poisson-gamma distributions are part of the EDM family, so can be used for modelling within the generalised linear models (GLMs) framework. This means that the fitting, model selection and residual analysis tools familiar from GLMs also apply to GLMs fitted to continuous data with exact zeros.

Biography

Peter is an Associate Professor in Biostatistics at the University of the Sunshine Coast, and routinely teaches introductory statistics to over 500 students over two semesters each year.

Peter has over 110 peer-reviewed research publications, has prepared numerous R packages available on CRAN (including the tweedie package, with almost 1 million downloads from CRAN) and co-developed the Dunn-Smyth (or quantile) residuals used in statistical modelling. Peter has been invited to give presentations on the R statistical environment at conferences and workshops across Australia.

Peter won an Australian Office of Learning and Teaching Citation in 2012, a student prize at the 16th International Workshop on Statistical Modelling in Denmark, and the EJ Pitman Prize for student talks at the Australian Statistics Conference in 2002. He has also published two textbooks: Generalized Linear Models With Examples in R (Springer) and Scientific Research and Methodology (CRS Press; also available as a free interactive online textbook).

Harnessing aerial imagery to overcome spatial complexity in yield trials
Zachary Aldiss
Abstract

Early-stage wheat breeding trials often suffer from low heritability because environmental noise, soil heterogeneity, and water gradients obscure true genetic potential. This study evaluates the integration of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS)-derived spectral data into spatial Linear Mixed Model (LMM) frameworks to account for residual variation and enhance genetic gain. Using data from 176 US wheat trials via a collaborative, NIFA-funded public breeding initiative, we fit univariate spatial LMMs and evaluated multitrait frameworks pairing grain yield with high-throughput phenotyping (HTP) latent variables and agronomic trait test weight used as a benchmark. Molecular data from 146 trials was further integrated to assess additive genetic variance partitioning. Our analysis affirms that HTP integration is a highly scalable strategy for reliability recovery, particularly across diverse breeding programs operating in spatially complex environments where traditional ANOVA-based methods struggle. By applying a standardized secondary trait from UAS imagery, we effectively recovered trial reliability in noisy environments where spatial trends otherwise dominate. Furthermore, the multitrait frameworks allowed for the extraction of biological signals from canopy spectral data, which successfully partitioned residual variation and improved the precision of variety effect estimation. However, our findings demonstrate that the value of HTP is strictly conditional on the baseline reliability of the trial, with diminishing returns observed in environments that already feature high univariate heritability.

Biography

I am a Postdoctoral Research Associate at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign with Dr Jessica Rutkoski.

Healing the History: A Robust Estimation Framework for Addressing Misidentification in POPAN Capture-Recapture Models
Adam Wong-Toi
Abstract

Following heavy 20th-century commercial whaling, Southern Hemisphere humpback whales have experienced rapid demographic recovery. Historically, monitoring relied on shore-based point censuses, which did not track individual life histories over time (Noad et al., 2020). Modern platforms, like Happywhale, collate fluke images to provide individual photo-identification. While these multi-decade datasets capture expansive longitudinal histories, they raise key analytical challenges. This study evaluates the vulnerability of open-population capture-recapture models (POPAN) to capture heterogeneity and misidentification errors. By applying both standard POPAN and finite-mixture ‘Capmix’ models to a 41-year dataset comprising 15,792 individual capture histories, we estimated contemporary population dynamics. Through simulation, the impact of individual misidentification is robustly quantified. To address this bias, an iterative stochastic reallocation algorithm was developed that uses the joint likelihood to reallocate misidentified “ghost” individuals to statistically plausible capture histories. In simulation, with a 1.5% per-image misidentification rate, the bias in the superpopulation size, N*, was approximately 7.2%, while survival and recruitment metrics remained stable. The iterative reallocation algorithm successfully reduced this abundance bias to 0.05%. Applying the framework to the Happywhale eastern Australian humpback whale data yielded a 2024 population estimate of 63,584 individuals, and an annual population growth rate of 10%, consistent with literature from land-based studies (Noad et al., 2020). This framework successfully corrects for misidentification bias when supplied with an estimated error rate from external matching validation exercises. It provides the necessary correction to citizen science datasets, securing a precise and structurally sound framework for long-term population modelling by healing the history.

Biography

Adam is a postgraduate Honours student in ecological statistics. He specialises in capture-recapture modelling for marine megafauna, including humpback and blue whales. His research focuses on developing robust estimation frameworks to mitigate misidentification bias to improve population abundance estimates.

15:45-16:00
Ensemble modelling and visualising uncertainty in fisheries stock assessments
Alise Fox
Abstract

Fisheries stock assessments play a central role in decision-making under uncertainty, informing management of complex ecological systems with significant social and economic consequences. A key challenge is not only quantifying uncertainty, but representing it in ways that are both statistically robust and accessible to stakeholders.

This presentation uses a recent stock assessment as a case study to examine how ensemble modelling and visualisation can improve the communication of uncertainty. In this assessment, spawning biomass was estimated from an ensemble of 12 plausible model scenarios rather than a single “best” model.

The ensemble approach allowed structural uncertainty—arising from assumptions about biology, data weighting and other model components—to be explicitly incorporated into final outputs. However, presenting the results of multiple models introduces challenges for interpretation, particularly when communicating to stakeholders with varying levels of statistical literacy.

I will present a range of strategies used to summarise ensemble outputs, including probability distributions of biomass and simplified summaries of scenario variability. These approaches aim to balance transparency with interpretability, ensuring that uncertainty is neither obscured nor overwhelming.

A key focus of the talk is how ensemble outputs reshape the role of visualisation and interpretation in applied statistics. Rather than supporting a single model narrative, visualisations must synthesise information across competing models, highlight robustness of conclusions, and reveal where uncertainty meaningfully affects decisions.

This work demonstrates that combining ensemble modelling with thoughtful visual design provides a powerful framework for communicating uncertainty in high-stakes applied contexts.

Biography

Alise Fox is a stock assessment scientist with Fisheries Queensland, applying statistics, mathematics, ecology and programming to support sustainable fisheries management. Her career spans research, teaching and science communication. Her work has been recognised through Superstars of STEM and a Queensland Women in STEM Prize. She’s passionate about making STEM accessible and inclusive.

16:00-16:15
Keeping the eastern king prawn stock assessment in line
Joanne Wortmann
Abstract

Commercial trawl vessels have changed considerably over time through the adoption of new and improved technologies and fishing gear. As a result, the relative fishing efficiency (or fishing power) of trawl vessels has been explicitly quantified in eastern king prawn stock assessments. A recently incorporated factor in estimating fishing power is line trawling behaviour. Line trawling occurs when a vessel trawls back and forth along the same path during a night, targeting specific areas where prawns are likely to aggregate. This behaviour can improve catchability by repeatedly targeting high-density patches, increasing the likelihood that prawns disturbed or missed in earlier passes are captured in subsequent trawls. This focused, iterative fishing strategy also exploits aggregating behaviour, effectively concentrating effort where catch rates are highest and reducing time spent searching. A linear mixed-effects model indicates that line trawling increases fishing efficiency, resulting in average catch increases of 11–19%. Catch and effort data used to derive the index of abundance in the eastern king prawn stock assessment are obtained from commercial logbooks (i.e. fishery–dependent data). It is therefore important to adjust for – that is, remove – the effects of changes in fishing power over time, so that trends in catch rates reflect changes in stock abundance rather than improvements in fishing efficiency. More generally, this work provides a case study in accounting for changes over time in how the data are collected, demonstrating how shifts in technology and behaviour can introduce bias into trends if not explicitly modelled.

Biography

Joanne Wortmann is a stock assessment scientist from Fisheries Queensland. Joanne was a maths lecturer at the University of Kwazulu-Natal in South Africa and before that Joanne was a data scientist for a medical insurance company.

16:15-16:30
Integrated Species Distribution Modeling for Fisheries Abundance Data: A Single Index Approach
Quan Vu
Abstract

In fisheries ecology, species abundance data are often collected by multiple surveys, each with unique characteristics. This article focuses on Atlantic sea scallop abundance data along the northeast coast of the United States, collected from two bottom trawl surveys which cover a larger spatial domain but have low catch efficiency, and a dredge survey which is more efficient but limited to domains where the species are believed to be present. To model such data, integrated species distribution models (ISDMs) have been proposed to incorporate information from multiple surveys, by including common environmental effects along with correlated survey-specific spatial fields. However, while flexible, these ISDMs can be susceptible to overfitting, which can complicate interpretability of the shared environmental effects and potentially lead to poor predictive performance. To overcome these drawbacks, we introduce a novel single index ISDM, built from a single index (with spatial random effects) that represents a latent measure of the true species distribution, and survey-specific catch efficiency functions which map the single index to the survey-specific expected catch. Our results show that the single index ISDM offers more meaningful interpretations of the environmental effects and survey catch efficiency differences, while potentially achieving better predictive performance than existing ISDMs. This is joint work with Francis Hui, Alan Welsh, Samuel Muller, Eva Cantoni, and Chris Haak.

Biography

Quan Vu is a Lecturer at the University of Sydney. His research focuses on developing statistical methods for complex spatial and spatio-temporal data, with an emphasis on addressing environmental and ecological problems. He specializes in the GLMM framework, using Gaussian processes, basis function models, and deep learning for spatial/spatio-temporal regression, prediction, and emulation.

09:05-09:20
Advanced Statistical Modelling and Sensor Technologies for Enhanced Animal Welfare Assessment
Chanatda Somchit
Abstract

Advanced statistical modelling plays a critical role in transforming high-volume sensor data into meaningful and actionable indicators of animal welfare. Sensor-based technologies are increasingly used to provide continuous, objective measures of animal health, behaviour, and welfare. Identifying behaviour and environmental thresholds beyond which animals begin to show signs of compromised health including heat stress and lameness is fundamental to effective monitoring and management. Equally important is the validation of accelerometer-based systems to ensure accurate behaviour classification. Statistical methodologies such as generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) including those developed for large-scale and giga datasets by Wood et al. (2015, 2017) are well suited to analysing complex, non-linear relationships among behaviour, environmental conditions, and health outcomes. These methods support the identification of risk thresholds for the early detection of welfare challenges and timely intervention. Complementary machine-learning techniques including decision tree algorithms provide robust and interpretable approaches for behaviour classification and sensor validation. Together, these analytical frameworks enable the extraction of reliable insights from complex datasets and support evidence-based decision-making. This presentation will highlight analytical frameworks that integrate advanced statistical and machine-learning methods with high-frequency sensor data to support animal welfare assessment. Case studies will demonstrate the application of GAMMs to identify environmental thresholds associated with heat stress and lameness in cattle, and the development of decision tree algorithms for behaviour classification in multi-species grazing ruminants using accelerometer data.

Biography

I have strong expertise in statistical methodologies, modelling, and their application to New Zealand primary sector research. With extensive experience in statistical programming using R, I have developed predictive modelling algorithms and advanced analytical approaches for large datasets helping pioneer their use in New Zealand agriculture and forestry research.

09:20-09:35
Teaching Clients to Catch Their Own Statistical Fish: Reflections on Building Statistical Capability Through Consulting
Alexandra Green
Abstract

At the Sydney Informatics Hub, I have recently experimented with a consulting approach inspired by the idea of teaching clients to catch their own statistical fish. Rather than repeatedly providing analyses, the goal is to help researchers move from “how do I do this?” to “I can do this myself”. This talk reflects on a series of one-to-one consultations with public health researchers who were primarily SPSS point-and-click users. The approach began with me leading an initial analysis and providing a reproducible R workflow. Rather than treating each new project as a separate engagement, that workflow became a template that could be adapted and extended as new research questions emerged. Existing analyses were modified to accommodate different outcome types, allowing clients to learn new statistical methods within a familiar analytical framework. Over time, clients developed both computational and statistical confidence. One client progressed from asking “How do I interpret this graph?” to “How can I fit a count model and assess whether zero inflation is required?”. Researchers increasingly ran analyses independently, adapted code for new projects, assessed model assumptions, and selected appropriate modelling approaches without me conducting the analysis. Shared, reproducible code also encouraged peer learning, with clients troubleshooting and building on one another’s work. I reflect on the trade-off between short-term efficiency and long-term capability building, and how reusable code, project-based learning, and progressive transfer of responsibility can support statistical literacy and independence. Finally, I consider whether a consulting engagement’s success might be measured not only by analyses completed, but by clients’ ability to complete the next one themselves.

Biography

Alexandra Green is a statistical consultant at the Sydney Informatics Hub with expertise in study design, epidemiology, meta-analysis, and applied statistics. Drawing on a background in animal sciences, she collaborates with researchers across disciplines to develop rigorous analytical approaches and reproducible workflows.

09:35-09:50
Version-Controlled Protocols and Equivalence Testing for Reproducible Drone Phenomics
Arden Burrell
Abstract

Across the Australian Plant Phenomics Network, drone phenotyping data are collected by different operators (network nodes), across multiple sites and years. These data are comparable only if every team collects, calibrates, and processes them the same way. The Airborne Phenomics Excellence project found that when operators repeat a drone flight or fly a shared target, results disagree, and the dominant, fixable cause is process, not sensors. The variance lived in field and processing procedure, and in whether the agreed method was written down, current, and followed. This presentation describes our response: managing scientific protocols the way software teams manage code, and then testing statistically whether they work.

Procedures live in a shared version-controlled repository, are revised through reviewed pull requests, locked as a published read-only wiki that teams follow in the field, and issued as tagged, citable releases, giving every dataset a permanent record of the method it was collected under.

But writing protocols down does not prove they deliver the comparability the network depends on. Conventional significance testing answers this poorly: failing to reject a difference is not evidence of equivalence, and with large pixel samples trivial differences become “significant”. In a controlled validation campaign, we frame cross-sensor calibration as a formal equivalence problem, deriving an equivalence bound and applying two one-sided tests (TOST) for mean reflectance, then assessing distributional equivalence (quantile TOST, Wasserstein distance, variance ratios) and a multivariate, classifier-based effect size across the visible-near-infrared and shortwave-infrared regions.

The result is a per-wavelength verdict (equivalent, non-equivalent, or inconclusive) showing where a procedure works and where recalibration is needed, a practical way to control variance and bias between operators, sites, and years that recur in multi-year, multi-site monitoring.

09:50-10:05
Integrating Spatial Data and On-Farm Experimentation to Analyse Wheat Variety Performance in Western Australia
Sandra Tanz
Abstract

On-farm experimentation (OFE) provides an opportunity to evaluate crop performance under commercial farming conditions while capturing the spatial variability inherent in production systems. However, this variability also presents statistical challenges for experimental design and analysis.

This pilot study investigates the integration of spatial data with large-scale OFE to better understand wheat variety performance across five grower-managed sites in Western Australia. Each trial was established within commercial paddocks using strip trial designs aligned with historical production zones. Two core wheat varieties, Scepter (a widely grown commercial cultivar) and Dale (a near-release InterGrain line) were included at all sites, with additional varieties incorporated where locally relevant.

The study focuses on developing and evaluating statistical methods that account for spatial variation by defining pseudo-environments using both equally spaced zones and environmental covariates derived from soil and topographic information. Trial analyses incorporate additional spatial datasets, including elevation and NDVI time series from drone and satellite imagery, to better characterise environmental heterogeneity and genotype-by-environment interactions.

The project aims to develop robust, spatially aware workflows for OFE trial design and analysis, encompassing data cleaning, spatial gridding, pseudo-environment assignment, and linear mixed modelling to account for spatial variation across commercial paddocks. By integrating spatial data, environmental covariates, and modern statistical methods, this work demonstrates the potential of OFE to complement conventional small-plot variety trials, improve variety evaluation, support agronomic decision-making, and contribute to predictive breeding in commercial farming systems.

Biography

Sandra Tanz is a Research Data Scientist at Curtin University, where she develops statistical and spatial analysis methods for on-farm experimentation in cereal breeding. She has a background in plant molecular biology and applied data science, with research interests in spatial statistics, mixed models, remote sensing, and the integration of environmental data into agricultural decision-making.

10:05-10:20
Bivariate analysis of ratio component traits in horticultural breeding programs
Ky Mathews
Abstract

Ratio traits are commonly used in agriculture as selection indices for complex characteristics. For example, flavour characteristics in strawberry are measured as a ratio of total soluble sugars to acidity, the so-called “brix-to-acid ratio”. In macadamia, fertility is measured as a ratio of the number of self-pollinated to open-pollinated florets on a raceme. The distributional properties of these ratio traits are often non-normal and heteroscedastic. For breeding decisions, selection on the component traits is also of interest and each has its own genetic variance that is ignored when incorporated into a ratio trait. In this study, we demonstrate a bivariate mixed-model approach for repeated measures, multi-year datasets is possible. Further, ancestral information is included to enable selection for variety release and for parents in future breeding cycles. Compared with direct univariate analysis of the derived ratio, the bivariate approach retains information on the component traits, quantifies their genetic relationship, and provides more interpretable outputs for selection of candidate varieties and future parents.

Biography

Ky is a Principal Biometrician at the Queensland Department of Primary Industries. She applies state-of-the-art statistical methods in plant breeding and pre-breeding programs. She is particularly interested in experimental design, spatial analyses, modelling genotype-by-environment interaction and incorporating pedigree and marker data in the linear mixed model framework.

10:20-10:35
Modelling stability of irrigated cotton farming system soil organic carbon content and function
Pauline Ding
Abstract

Long-term changes in stocks and stability within irrigated cotton farming systems in semi-arid Australia is of great public interest. Soil organic carbon underpins nutrient cycling, soil structural stability, and ecosystem resilience, yet soil organic carbon responses to crop rotation and diversification in irrigated Vertosols remain uncertain.

In this project, archived soil samples were collected between 1995 and 2020 from a long-term farming systems experiment at the Australian Cotton Research Institute, Narrabri, NSW. Treatments included continuous cotton and cotton rotated with wheat, vetch, or faba bean under minimum tillage management. The experiment commenced in 1995 in the West Field with five cropping treatments replicated four times. The following year, 1996, three additional treatments added in adjacent East Field, where the cotton phase occurred 12 months latter than the West Field. Soil samples were collected at 30cm, 60cm and 90 cm depth and analysed using dry combustion and near-infrared spectroscopy. In this study, we use linear mixed model to fit multivariate long-term soil collections and evaluate long-term soil carbon dynamics in intensive agricultural systems. This is a joint work with CISRO Agriculture and Food.

Biography

Pauline is a Lecturer in Statistics at the University of Wollongong. She has a strong portfolio of interdisciplinary research in public health, medicine, and the social sciences. More recently, Pauline has developed a passion for agricultural soil studies, inspired by the 29 heads of cattle on the family farm.

Keynote #6 - Dr. Ruth Butler
Chair: Vanessa Cave
Details
Consulting in the real world: reflections, comments and data
Dr. Ruth Butler
Abstract

I have worked as a statistical consultant for a long time now, working primarily in Agriculture and Horticulture science institutes. Along the way, I have developed some strong opinions about statistics and how statisticians work. I will discuss some of these. I will then present a couple of relatively recent pieces of work, each with a statistical challenge.

Biography

Dr. Ruth Butler has worked as a biometrician/statistical consultant for more than 35 years, initially in the UK, then from the mid-1990s in New Zealand. She has primarily worked with bio-protection scientists (plant pathology, entomology), but also has significant experience working with other non-medical biological scientists including in soils/agronomy, food research and plant breeding. Ruth has been a Genstat user throughout her career, contributing around 10 Genstat procedures, and has been a beta tester of Genstat for 30 years. Ruth has also been a CycDesigN user since the very first version was released in 1997. Her interests are in good data management practices, well-designed experiments, and in improving communication between statisticians and scientists.
